member of the commission. − mr president, i would first like to thank the committee on international trade (inta) and its rapporteur, mr zalewski, for this excellent report on the commission’s regulation on financial responsibility for investor-state dispute settlements. this is the third of three pillars of the eu’s investment policy. in this respect, i acknowledge parliament’s own request in april 2011 for the commission to legislate in the area of financial responsibility. turning to the inta report, the commission is, in general terms, ready to accept the bulk of parliament’s amendments, either as drafted or subject to some further work on drafting. we are mainly concerned with those amendments which make it more difficult for the commission to act to defend the union’s interests, in particular some elements of amendments 19, 27, 28 and 30. to give just one example, the commission must be able to act simply when there is a risk to the interpretation of future agreements. adding ‘serious’ makes it more difficult for the commission to act to protect the union’s interests. i raise this point because this regulation gives member states power to defend themselves – and also, effectively, the eu – on the international stage. it means that a member state on its own can offer interpretations of an eu agreement. however, these are no longer individual member state agreements which affect only one member state but agreements concluded at eu level affecting the eu, all the other member states and all eu investors. moreover, interpretation in one case will clearly have an effect on other cases which may involve eu institutions, other member states and eu investors abroad. developments in the council might put this in doubt. we hope that parliament will support the commission in defending the unity of external representation in order to protect eu interests. as i said, this is a very important proposal which will put in place a framework for years to come. while seemingly complex, it involves some key institutional questions which i trust parliament will, like the commission, seek to protect. let me now turn to the oral question. the commission agrees that bilateral and investment treaties (bits) between eu member states do not comply with eu law. they have been challenged before national courts. these proceedings are still pending and there also seems to be widespread agreement among member states that at least a lack of legal certainty persists. all the member states except one have such intra-eu bits in force. commission officials have therefore initiated informal discussions with them with a view to reaching agreement on the joint termination of all these agreements within an agreed time frame. several member states have already agreed bilaterally to terminate their agreements, and the commission has encouraged them to proceed with doing so. however, in those cases where member states are not willing to terminate agreements, the commission is ready to play its role as a guardian of the treaties so as to ensure compliance with eu law. the european court of justice ruled in 2009 that provisions in the bilateral investment agreements of austria, sweden and finland relating to the free transfer of capital were in breach of the eu treaties and did not allow for the application of eu measures on the restriction of capital movements. the member states concerned have been compelled to bring their agreements into compliance with their treaty obligations or to denounce them. the 2012 regulation establishing transitional arrangements for bilateral and investment agreements between member states and third countries specifies that, where an existing investment agreement conflicts with substantive union law, the member state concerned has to request authorisation from the commission to open renegotiation of such an agreement with a view to bringing it into compliance with eu law. when formally authorising the renegotiation of an investment agreement, the commission instructs the member state concerned to amend it to ensure compatibility with substantive union law, in particular through provisions ensuring that nothing in the agreement prevents the member state concerned from fulfilling its obligations under eu law. when the negotiations are over, the member state has to notify the commission of the final outcome of its negotiations and, before authorising its signature, the commission carries out a final verification of whether the conditions established in regulation (eu) no 1219/2012 have been met. under this regulation, member states can also be allowed to negotiate and conclude under certain conditions new bilateral investment agreements with third countries. only agreements which are compatible with eu law can be authorised. this process of authorising member states to negotiate or sign new agreements or to renegotiate existing ones has only just started, with 29 requests so far for authorisation to sign or allow the entry into force of protocols amending existing bits and 36 requests to open negotiations to amend existing bits. the commission is now issuing its first authorisations and we are keeping parliament duly informed. the commission also ensures that eu investment agreements being negotiated at eu level are also fully in line with eu law. a specific reference to this objective is included in the recommendations for negotiating directives which the commission has addressed to council and which have been shared with parliament. let me, finally, reassure you that the level of investment protection afforded by future investment agreements to foreign investors will be in line with general principles common to eu and member state law. there is a broad consensus among eu institutions and all the relevant stakeholders that one of the main objectives of eu investment policy is to provide enhanced legal certainty and a high level of protection for investors in line with the best practices of eu member states. these practices reflect not only fundamental principles of international law but also general principles that are common to the eu and its member states’ legal systems, such as the principles of non-discrimination, the rule of law, access to justice, due process and the obligation to fully compensate in the event of expropriation. these are precisely the main elements and standards that we are covering in the eu investment protection agreements. parliament suggested in its 2011 resolution on the future european international investment policy that the breadth of interpretation left to arbitral tribunals should be reduced in order to increase legal certainty and better protect the public intervention domain. the commission has endorsed this view and is endeavouring to better clarify the content of our investment protection standards without reducing the level of protection, for example by including useful guidance on the practice of arbitral tribunals. as this is a joint debate on some rather detailed issues, i have spoken at length and did so to clarify the rationale for the commission’s proposal. i look forward to parliament’s support.

in writing. − myanmar/burma's access to gsp tariff preferences was temporarily suspended in 1997 by council regulation (ec) no 552/97 due to the systematic and widespread practice of forced labour, confirmed by the international labour organisation in a special procedure of its committee of inquiry. however, a new report by the ilo commission of inquiry has shown that the practices leading to such suspension have now ceased, and i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − the european union's generalised system of preferences (gsp) offers developing countries a reduction in customs duties, i.e. trade preferences for exporters from these countries, ensuring that they pay lower duties on some or all of the products exported to the european market. the objective of this policy is to contribute to a better integration of the beneficiary countries into world trade and thus to contribute to their economic development, while respecting human rights and the principles of sustainable development. however, serious and systematic violations of the human rights conventions of the united nations (un) and the international labour organisation (ilo) may result in the temporary suspension of preferential arrangements as provided for in regulation (ec) no 552/97. the confirmation in 1997 of the systematic and widespread practice of forced labour in myanmar/burma led to the suspension of the non-reciprocal tariff preferences regime between the republic of myanmar and the eu. since then, the commission has identified genuine efforts to open up and reform the labour market and therefore considers that the conditions for restoring access to the generalized tariff preferences for myanmar/burma are met.
in writing. − the generalized preferences regulation (gsp) with burma/myanmar was suspended in 1997 by the council due to the continued use and practice of forced labour, confirmed by the international labour organisation. however, in view of the gradual change in practice, the commission intends to reinstate the gsp. burma/myanmar is facing a crucial period of transition to democracy. the gsp and the 'everything but arms' mechanism are of the utmost importance for the development of economic activities in this country. however, forced labour still exists and must be completely banned, and the union must therefore continue to monitor this.
in writing. − myanmar's access to eu tariff preferences (gsp) was temporarily suspended in 1997 due to the systematic and widespread practice of forced labour, confirmed by the international labour organisation (ilo) in a special procedure of its commission of inquiry. it was then determined that the temporary suspension should end following a report from the commission demonstrating that the practices leading to that suspension have ceased. the european commission now concludes that the breaches cannot be considered 'serious and systematic' any longer, which means that the tariff preferences should be reinstated, in accordance with the current gsp regulation. despite the progress made, doubts remain on the question of forced labour, among others, reinforced by the complaints of some trade unions, which has given rise to reservations in our group about the reintroduction of gsp preferences.
in writing. - i approve this report, taking into account that the european union, when negotiating investment protection agreements with third countries, including canada, the united states, japan or india and china, allows for an investor dispute settlement mechanism which will allow companies to bring their complaints against the european union in the event of a breach of the key provisions of the agreement. despite the disagreement among member states who want to continue to have more powers in these matters, i believe we should follow the community line, expressing my strong support already now for a stronger role for the commission in defending investor arbitration cases.
in writing. − the lisbon treaty has placed foreign direct investment within the eu's common commercial policy, a matter of exclusive eu competence. as we said in the debate, this is a problem which must be solved, sooner rather than later, by overturning this and other provisions of an illegitimate treaty which has escaped the democratic scrutiny of the people. this regulation aims to make the necessary adjustments, taking into account the numerous bilateral investment treaties between eu member states and third countries signed before the entry into force of the lisbon treaty. it establishes a framework for the distribution of responsibilities between the eu and the member states in the various conflict situations. the key principle is that the financial responsibility arising from investor-state dispute resolution proceedings should be assigned to the agent who granted dispute settlement. in cases where the treatment in question is granted by the eu institutions, the financial responsibility should lie with the eu institutions. in addition to our principled position against the exclusive competence of the eu in this area, there are several unacceptable provisions in this proposal for a regulation which constrain the member states in defending their legitimate interests by subordinating them to the so-called interests of the union. we know what interests are involved.
in writing. − with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the union acquired exclusive competence for the conclusion of international agreements on investment protection. the union is already a party to an agreement on investor-state dispute settlement (the energy charter treaty) and will seek to negotiate such provisions in a number of agreements currently under negotiation or to be negotiated in the future. it is therefore necessary to consider how to manage the financial consequences of such disputes. this regulation aims to establish the framework for the management of those consequences. the central organising principle of this regulation is that the financial responsibility arising from investor-state dispute settlement proceedings should be assigned to the agent who granted the disputed treatment. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties on the alleged lack of cooperation from the union institutions. in cases where the treatment in question is granted by a member state of the european union, the financial responsibility should lie with that member state.
in writing. - as requested by the rapporteur for the present case, i voted in favour of referring to the committee on international trade the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a framework for the management of financial liability relating to investor-state dispute settlement bodies set up by international agreements to which the european union is a party, in order to initiate a new trilogue.

in writing. the report under consideration, drawn up by mr horst schnellhardt, deals with the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the non-commercial movement of pet animals. the movement of pet animals has been regulated since 2003 by regulation (ec) no 998/2003 and subsequent amendments. however, in recent years, pet movements have undergone changes. the commission and the member states have carried out successful rabies vaccination campaigns, which suggests that rabies is now in principle extinct in many regions of the union. it is still important to ensure a high level of safety with regard to potential risks to public and animal health, while at the same time making life easier for pet owners who wish to travel with their animals in the european union or in third countries. i also think it is important to combat the fraudulent and disguised non-commercial movement of dogs, cats and sometimes ferrets for commercial purposes, in order to circumvent the application of stricter rules on the marketing and import of these animals.
in writing. − the main objective of the proposed regulation is to make life easier for pet owners who wish to travel with their animals in the european union or in third countries, taking into account a high level of safety with regard to potential risks to public and animal health. one of the inherent concerns is the alleged commercial movement of dogs, cats and sometimes ferrets, often fraudulently disguised as non-commercial movement in order to circumvent the application of stricter rules and hence a maximum of five animals per traveller. the current provisions allow member states to grant special derogations from the mandatory rabies vaccination for dogs, cats and ferrets less than three months old, since it is veterinary inadvisable to vaccinate these young animals. however, there are uncertainties regarding the time between vaccination and full immunisation, raising concerns when travelling with animals less than 12 weeks of age. some additional information is also suggested to improve the identification of the animal concerned and to better prevent the falsification of identification documents. we voted in favour.
in writing. − this proposal repeals and replaces regulation (ec) no 998/2003 of the european parliament and of the council laying down the animal health requirements governing the non-commercial movement of pet animals and amending council directive 92/65/eec. it lays down the animal health conditions to be observed in the case of non-commercial movements of pet animals into a member state from another member state or from third countries and the rules for the control of such movements. it aims to ensure a sufficient level of safety with regard to the risks to public and animal health involved in such non-commercial movements and to remove any unjustified obstacles to such movements.

in writing. - this resolution follows the european commission's communication on ex ante coordination of the plans for major economic policy reforms in the eu published on 20 march. attention is drawn to the need to implement economic reforms in the member states (ms) that promote sustained economic growth. these reforms must be coordinated, contribute to the prosperity of the countries where they are implemented, foster positive synergies in all other ems and be based on solidarity and cohesion mechanisms. in the legislative proposals on economic coordination, the involvement of the social partners and the involvement of national and european parliaments are also fundamental and mechanisms should be created to integrate all member states into these processes. the european commission's proposed competitiveness and convergence instrument should take account of the needs of each member state and be designed around strategies for long-term sustainable growth and reducing disparities, based on budgetary capacity made available for this purpose. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. - i believe that, beyond its economic importance, the restitution of property stolen by former dictators and their regimes to the countries in transition in the arab spring is a moral and legal imperative and a highly political issue, because of its implications in terms of restoring justice and accountability in the spirit of democracy and the rule of law, and it substantiates the political commitment and credibility of the eu, thus constituting an essential element of the union's partnership with its southern neighbours, in particular egypt, libya and tunisia. for the arab spring countries, the recovery of stolen goods is also of economic and social importance, as funds are needed to stabilise economies and create jobs and growth in these countries, which are facing serious economic challenges.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution which stresses the need to improve cooperation between the main actors at national and international level on the supervision of the return of goods and ensuring that returned goods are used in a transparent and effective manner in the requesting countries.
in writing. − the recovery of illicitly acquired assets, currently frozen in a number of third countries, is a lengthy and complex judicial procedure. however, this same recovery of assets, when carried out in a transparent and effective manner, is not only a privileged vehicle for a strong message against the impunity of criminals involved in corruption and money laundering, but also a tool for economic recovery of countries harmed by dictatorial regimes. in the wake of the arab revolution, the european union immediately froze the assets of former dictators and their families and other people associated with the regimes. now is the time to ensure that the assets misappropriated by deposed dictators and their regimes can be returned to the countries concerned. this motion for a resolution aims to raise awareness among the international actors concerned of the need to make significant efforts to achieve the objectives of asset recovery. i voted in favour.
in writing. − beyond its economic importance, the restitution of property stolen by former dictators and their regimes to countries in transition from the arab spring is a moral and legal imperative and a highly political issue, due to its implications in terms of restoring justice and accountability in the spirit of democracy and the rule of law. i also recognize that for the arab spring countries, the recovery of stolen goods is equally of economic and social importance, as funds are needed to stabilise the economies and create jobs and growth in these countries, which are facing serious economic challenges. for the reasons i have just given, i voted in favour of the joint resolution by the european parliament.

in writing. - the creation of bosnia-herzegovina, following the destabilisation and war in the balkans, resulted from the dismemberment of the republic of yugoslavia, a process which resulted in thousands of victims and which destroyed the economic structure of yugoslavia. after 14 years, bosnia-herzegovina is still a nato protectorate, as demonstrated by statements made by the un representative for bosnia-herzegovina on 14 may, according to which the european union and nato military missions in the country continue to assure citizens that the country is safe, despite the difficult political situation. the task of ensuring that all sides continue to comply with the dayton peace agreement also remains. after 14 years, the governance of bosnia and herzegovina continues to require an international presence, the eu presence is reinforced, the mandate of the european union multinational stabilisation force (eufor althea), a mission voted by this parliament in november 2004, is renewed. this was the result of the interference of the western powers in the region. the consequences are and will continue to be felt by the populations.
in writing. - bosnia and herzegovina remains committed to eu membership, which would be a great benefit for all its citizens. the holding of peaceful, free and fair local elections was an important step in this direction. however, there are still areas which need to be improved in order to progress towards full membership.

in writing. − since 1971, the eu has granted non-reciprocal trade preferences to developing countries, ensuring that exporters from these countries pay lower duties on some or all of the products they export to the eu. this gives them vital access to eu markets, which contributes to the growth of their economies. this system is known as the "generalised system of preferences". this system had been suspended for myanmar/burma due to the widespread practice of forced labour in that country. however, efforts made by myanmar/burma in this regard may lead to the re-establishment of the generalized system of preferences for that country. we must therefore monitor the evolution of the existence of forced labour in myanmar/burma in order to consider the possible re-establishment of the generalized system of preferences in the future.

in writing. - macro-regions are the logical consequence of the growing interdependence of countries and their similar or common characteristics, underlying a membership of a particular geographical and cultural area which, if it transcends borders, is nevertheless delimited by them. the macro-regional approach allows common problems to be faced, shared problems to be tackled, cohesion to be promoted and solutions to be sought whose effects can benefit all actors and give the european union an overall vision that allows it to develop its action more appropriately. considering that the territories that make up the alpine region have many common features, such as the unique geographical character of their high-altitude mountain areas, and are strongly interlinked with heterogeneous economic capacities and growing concerns about environmental issues, demographic developments, transport infrastructure, tourism and energy issues, i think that the region will only gain from a global and macro-regional approach such as the one proposed here.
in writing. the alps are the only high mountain area which has been populated for many years and whose importance for the development of the european union is undeniable. despite its potential, it has experienced a significant decline in its agricultural production which protected certain areas and a flight of people to the cities. this is a situation that must be reversed. to do this, it is necessary to know how to take advantage of existing natural resources by implementing development projects in the areas of agriculture, transport and tourism. the peripheral and outermost regions need similar attention from the european institutions in order to increase their competitiveness and create conditions for the settlement of their population. i voted in favour of this joint motion for a resolution, tabled pursuant to rule 115 (5) and rule 110 (4) of the rules of procedure, replacing the motions for resolutions tabled by the epp, s&d, greens/efa and alde political groups, on the need to establish a macro-regional strategy for the alps because i consider this strategy to be essential to the development of this territory with a direct impact on the development of the eu itself and i hope that in the future other mountain regions will be able to benefit from a similar development strategy.
in writing. − this resolution considers that large-scale strategies, such as macro-regional strategies, are a plus for the implementation of eu policies at local and regional level, emphasising governance at various levels for their implementation. it also proposes to apply this formula to the alps, in line with the strategies adopted for the baltic sea and the danube. we welcome the concern to promote policies that promote effective economic, social and territorial cohesion in the european union and involve cooperation between countries and regions with different affinities, taking account in particular of their specific characteristics and natural constraints. however, part of the framework for this macro-regional strategy is set in the framework of the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy, with which we disagree and whose consequences for countries and populations have generally been: worsening of working conditions, increasing unemployment and favouring the concentration of capital in the hands of monopoly holders. the document presents contradictory aspects, including the way in which the eu subverts the concept of cohesion by tying countries to strategies whose aims and objectives are in contradiction to those of the desired cohesion.
in writing. − the macro-regional strategies are designed to make better use of existing resources to address territorial development issues, identify common responses to common challenges, strengthen territorial integration and increase the effectiveness of the various forms of eu-supported policies and partnerships between public administrations and local authorities, as well as other institutions and civil society organisations. the development of large-scale strategies such as macro-regional strategies should contribute to strengthening the role of the local and regional level in the implementation of eu policies and the principle of multi-level governance should be placed at the heart of the planning and implementation of the alpine strategy. the macro-regional strategy for the alps is an effective instrument for strengthening european territorial cooperation in the region concerned, applying a bottom-up approach and enhancing cooperation through better use of available resources, thus facilitating cross-sectoral policy coordination.

mr president, there is a fallacious assumption which often frames the debates we have here on consumer protection policy. this assumption is that the deeper the single market, the deeper the successive liberalising agendas of the european union, the deeper the competition, the more consumer rights will be safeguarded. but reality exposes this fallacy. the reality is that liberalization and privatization have harmed and continue to harm consumers. energy, transport, financial services, and others, are stark examples. the liberalization and deregulation of agricultural and trade policies have also harmed consumers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's food safety is not compromised. it is therefore time to correct the foundations on which this debate is based, to bring them into line with reality, if we want a genuine defence of consumer rights and not just to use them as misleading propaganda for other purposes.

member of the commission. − mr president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mrs delli, for the report. it is a particularly timely initiative given the increasingly restricted access to affordable housing triggered by the crisis, as well as the rising levels of poverty and homelessness in the european union. having a suitable home is a precondition for a productive, dignified life. while planning and implementing housing policies remains primarily a matter of national competence, the commission fully supports the efforts of member states in this domain. the recently adopted social investment package, for instance, contains a number of relevant provisions related to housing. first, it calls on member states to foster social inclusion through providing quality, affordable and accessible essential services, including social housing, and thus reinforcing the message of the 2008 recommendation on active inclusion. second, member states are offered eu support to develop a methodology for reference budgets enabling a decent standard of living. further, the commission has invited member states to put into place integrated housing policies in order to better meet housing needs and thus prevent homelessness. the social investment package also seeks to mobilise member states to spend european union funds in a more strategic way. european union funds are indeed available to improve housing outcomes, and housing remains a funding priority for the next financial framework of 2014-2020. the european regional development fund may, for instance, finance integrated housing interventions and energy-efficient renovations. the european social fund can complement such integrated investments, and funds enhanced access to social services. the commission provides information on housing policy developments, as appropriate, in the context of the european semester exercise. some member states have already received country-specific recommendations on housing and social housing in 2012 and 2013. as underlined in ms delli’s report, well-designed housing policies, including social housing policies, may usefully contribute to progressing towards important european union policy goals. these goals may encompass poverty reduction, promoting active inclusion and inclusive territorial urban development, combating climate change, improving health and consumer policy outcomes or avoiding macroeconomic imbalances. however, careful policy planning is needed in the member states to avoid speculative real-estate bubbles and to intelligently channel housing support and investments with due regard to the resources available. housing policies should be seen in a wider context and built on a balanced mix of measures, such as investment in infrastructure, housing support or a responsible loan policy. given these considerations and the ambitious agenda presented in ms delli’s report, the commission will reflect on the concrete suggestions of the proposal at a later stage, following a more in-depth analysis of the report.
the policies of the european union have led to an increase in social inequalities, unemployment, poverty and the population at risk of poverty. more and more people and families are being denied the right to housing. in this context, investment in the social housing sector is a pressing social need that is gaining in importance. the right to housing, enshrined in the constitution in some countries, such as portugal, should be realised by guaranteeing citizens and families adequate housing, meeting their needs and ensuring their well-being, privacy and quality of life, thus contributing to social justice and cohesion and combating social exclusion and poverty. housing policies must combat solutions which lead to social exclusion and spatial segregation of certain sections of the population. social housing should be seen as a means of overcoming situations of social exclusion and not as a perpetuation of these situations. it is necessary to diagnose new social realities, recognising that the socio-family profiles of those using social housing have changed, as has the demand for such housing. these concerns should be duly addressed in the next multiannual financial framework (2014-2020), in particular in the cohesion funds.
member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, i would like to thank the committee on legal affairs and the rapporteur for this excellent report and for its constant support of our policies of removing the obstacles to full enjoyment by europeans of their benefits as eu citizens. we discussed today the application of an important instrument to allow european citizens to effectively exert their right of access to justice in other member states – the 2003 directive on legal aid in cross-border civil and commercial matters. the 2012 commission report on its application observes that all the member states which are bound by the directive have transposed it. no major problems of implementation have been observed, even if there are some differences of interpretation between member states. the fact that there has only been one case before the european court of justice concerning cross-border legal aid also indicates that the application of the directive from a legal point of view is satisfactory. however, both the parliament and the commission reports conclude that awareness among citizens and lawyers of the benefits of this directive must be improved. the commission is already taking steps to that end: the e-justice portal is currently being updated in order to improve access to information and to the standard forms for legal aid. the migration of the european judicial network website to the e-justice portal will further improve user-friendliness and provide comprehensive and updated information. this will also inform citizens better regarding the other european procedures such as the european small claims procedure and the european order for payment procedure. in addition, the commission has developed a compendium of legislation in cross-border civil and commercial matters, which includes this directive. the compendium has been distributed to legal professionals in member states on several occasions. coming to legal professionals and their role in applying the directive: not long ago in this very chamber, we highlighted the importance of judicial training in the application of eu law. we should help lawyers become familiar with the possibilities offered by the directive and advise citizens accordingly. we are implementing the pilot project on judicial training put forward by parliament. we are also providing funding, for example for the establishment of the european training platform. our proposals for the next financial framework also include judicial training as a priority area in order to support member states in their efforts. coming to the role of the member states: as you highlighted in your report, they must do their share of informing their own citizens about their rights under mr president, the european union's rules on so-called state aid are one of the most immediate ways of curbing democratic state intervention in the economy. this restriction can only be understood as an attack on democracy itself, to open the door to the dictatorship of the market. significantly, however, these rules do not prevent the channelling of generous public resources to powerful private interests. this is the case of multinationals, which the european union continues to allow, a few years after receiving large amounts of public funding, to move to other places in search of more public support, leaving a trail of destruction and unemployment behind them. the limitations on state intervention are particularly damaging to the less developed regions, preventing them from overcoming the distance which separates them from the other more developed regions. real economic and social cohesion and the fight against inequalities require public planning and intervention which, as experience has shown, do not meet these rules.
mr president, road infrastructure must respond to obvious economic and social needs for the transport and mobility of people and goods. needs that cannot be dissociated from a specific regional and territorial context. these specificities must obviously weigh on the type of operation and functioning of each infrastructure, including whether or not tolls are introduced and who is or is not liable to pay them. in portugal, for example, the introduction of tolls on road infrastructure, particularly motorways, in regions where they did not previously exist has proved disastrous, with considerable damage to regional development, the local economy, smes, citizens' mobility and road safety itself. moreover, it is now known that a substantial part of the revenue generated goes to cover the costs of the toll system itself. these are facts which cannot be ignored in this debate, nor can the experience of public-private partnerships, which has proved disastrous and ruinous for the public interest, be ignored.
madam president, to talk about food is to talk about health. we must protect consumers and end misleading food labelling. for example, references to gluten-free or lactose-free must be reliable because they have implications for people's health. i think that the agreement reached with the council is a positive one overall, because it clarifies the scope of the regulation and prevents certain operators from marketing food as special when in fact it is not and does not comply with the requirements laid down in the legislation. restrictions on the use of images of infants in labelling and advertising, which may create an idealised impression of the use of a particular product, are also positive. in addition, the agreement guarantees the revision of the requirements on residues, pesticides, labelling, advertising, commercial practices, etc. which concern infant formula, which is indeed very positive.
madam president, this regulation deals with specific provisions relating to food intended for specific vulnerable groups, such as infants and young children or people with medical problems. in this area, no other criterion is acceptable than that of ensuring the maximum possible protection of these groups, the maximum protection of human health and the strict application of principles such as the precautionary principle. it is also imperative to use the utmost transparency and to ensure that all relevant information is provided to the consumer. among the various aspects covered by this regulation, we would like to stress the importance of making further progress in the future in limiting or prohibiting the presence of residues of certain pesticides. this is an area where existing legislation must be constantly in line with the best available knowledge, and everything must be done to improve this knowledge. public research and development institutions and state laboratories play a key role in this area in supporting the formulation of appropriate public policies to safeguard the public interest. this is a role which, for various reasons, the european food safety authority is not in a position to play on its own.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the goal of the europe 2020 strategy is very clear: to lift 20 million people out of poverty. but what is happening is just the opposite. the crisis has exacerbated poverty and social exclusion across the union. commissioner andor is well aware of this dramatic situation and knows that it is time to give a clear political message to the citizens. in my country, portugal, about 20% of the population lives in poverty, and the number of portuguese who spend the whole day without eating has increased by 44% in the last three years. last year, 8 million kilos of food were distributed in portugal by the solidarity institutions. this aid fund, like other european funds, should be compulsory and its financing should not be less than eur 3.5 billion. this corresponds to the amount allocated to its predecessor, the european food distribution programme, negotiated before the crisis began. it is not reasonable that in the social context in which we live, the funding of this fund should be reduced. all member states are experiencing poverty, as evidenced by the number of countries participating in the european food distribution programme, which increased from 9 participants in 2001 to 20 in 2012. we must not forget the european union's core values of solidarity and social cohesion. the crisis must not divert us from these values. on the contrary, we must stand together in the fight against exclusion and poverty.
mr president, today more than yesterday - and, we hope, more than tomorrow - given the economic and social crisis we are going through, all initiatives to assist the most deprived are urgent. after the threats of ending the food aid programme without any follow-up, the european fund for the most deprived proposes a different aid which should be better adapted to the needs of individuals and families. i would point out, however, that this fund has a low budget for the real difficulties faced by european citizens and is out of step with the growth rate of poverty in the euro area, as it aims to support only 4 million citizens out of a total of 120 million potential beneficiaries. we must now do more with less, be more responsible in the management of funds and, above all, we must end the cycle of poverty, which is often associated with unlimited support or reciprocity. it is also necessary to monitor the strict and thrifty implementation of this fund, ensuring that it does not compete with other support or duplicate existing responses.

in writing. - i support this report, stressing that although the data provided by the european commission indicate a change in implementation by the member states, the truth is that citizens' awareness of their rights under this directive is very limited, and it is necessary for european citizens to actually know their rights at european union level as european citizens. i therefore believe that procedures should be simplified so that citizens can have access to legal aid without the help of a foreign lawyer, and pro bono services should also be developed.
in writing. − directive 2003/8/ec of 27 january 2003 on improving access to justice in crossborder disputes by establishing common minimum rules on legal aid in such disputes is an important piece of legislation for european citizens, which aims to ensure that people with fewer resources also have access to justice in other member states. in 2012, the european commission presented the first evaluation report on the application of the directive, concluding that all member states are, overall, successfully implementing the directive. the main problem identified is that it is very little known. only 12% of citizens are aware of the existence of cross-border legal aid, which means that citizens do not benefit from this right. it is therefore important to take measures to ensure greater awareness of cross-border legal aid, in particular among legal professionals. in order to improve the levels of competence, member states should consider designating a single authority in charge of transmission and reception in each jurisdiction, thus ensuring that the officials in charge of these cases have sufficient experience. i therefore support this report.
in writing. − in a true european area of justice, every citizen should be able to go to the courts and authorities in any member state as easily as in their own country, so it is important to remove any obstacles that may hinder access to justice. in this regard, a directive was adopted in 2003 with the aim of improving access to justice in cross-border disputes in civil and commercial matters by establishing common minimum rules ensuring the possibility of access to legal aid, in particular for citizens who do not have sufficient resources, such as representation by a lawyer, interpretation and translation charges, etc. almost ten years after its entry into force, i am pleased that the principle of crossborder legal aid itself has been successfully implemented in all member states, with only a few practical problems. however, the number of people who have benefited from it is quite small and it is regrettable that this added value is not being fully exploited due to the low level of awareness not only among citizens (only 12%) but also among professionals and national legal aid services. the necessary measures must be taken urgently to ensure that both citizens and professionals are made more aware of the problem.
in writing. − in a community that increasingly integrates aspects of its common life, crossborder disputes will tend to increase. this situation poses an unavoidable challenge to national courts and the european union to ensure that the right to legal aid also applies in these cases and is sufficiently known to citizens who may need it. the increasingly cross-border nature of legal relations will require an adequate response capacity on the part of national institutions and judicial officers, who will be more exposed to the need to deepen their knowledge of languages and of the law in force in other member states of the union. this interpenetration of legal systems will require greater demands on legal aid providers, who should be given specific training and preparation to enable them to carry out their work with a high degree of knowledge and professionalism, so as to ensure that the interests of those who will use them are adequately protected.
in writing. − article 47 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union states that every person whose rights and freedoms guaranteed by union law have been violated has the right to bring an action before a court in accordance with the provisions of this article. (...) legal aid is granted to persons who lack sufficient resources, in so far as such aid is necessary to ensure effective access to justice. improving access to justice in the eu, including through legal support in crossborder civil and commercial litigation, is the subject of this report by mr tadeus zwiefka. if at national level the interpretation of the law is confusing, in the case of crossborder disputes it becomes much more complicated. i therefore welcome all the efforts being made by the european institutions to simplify and harmonise legislation so that justice is quicker, more effective and less burdensome. i voted in favour of this proposal for a revision of the crossborder litigation directive because by boosting consumer confidence we are increasing crossborder trade and driving economic growth. i also call for this regulation to be widely disseminated (only 12% of european citizens were aware of it) so that all those who need it can benefit from legal support.
in writing. − this report calls on the commission to make some amendments to directive 2003/8/ec on improving access to justice in crossborder disputes by establishing common minimum rules on legal aid in such disputes. the rapporteur advocates, among other measures, the clarification of the european procedures to which the directive also applies; the clarification of differences of interpretation between member states; the dissemination to citizens of the right to cross-border legal aid; the development of databases of legal professionals with linguistic and comparative law knowledge; the defence of special training schemes. member states are encouraged to ensure the availability of pre-litigation legal aid and are called upon to sign and/or ratify the hague convention on international access to justice. the objective of ensuring that all citizens, including the poorest, also have access to justice in other member states when exercising their right to free movement is both fair and relevant. however, we distance ourselves from some of the solutions proposed in the report, such as the existence of a single competent authority for crossborder legal assistance or the prevalence of the definition of civil or commercial matters in eu law over the definition of member states.

in writing. − legal aid should be granted only to persons whose financial resources do not allow them to access justice. considering that the thresholds for financial resources have different definitions in the various member states of the european union, and in order to facilitate procedures for both citizens and the authorities implementing the directive, citizens should be able to choose, in the case of cross-border requests for legal aid, between their member state of residence or the member state in which the court operates. cross-border legal aid also covers, in accordance with the directive, the additional costs involved, such as interpretation, translation and travel expenses. only the correct application of directive 2003/8/ec and awareness raising about the right to cross-border legal aid can ensure that eu citizens exercise their right to free movement and benefit from the internal market. in view of the third paragraph of article 47 of the tfeu, which provides for legal aid for those who lack sufficient resources, i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution which proposes improvements in this area in the context of crossborder civil and commercial proceedings.

in writing. − i approve this report, considering that measures should be taken to ensure that lawyers appointed in such cases have adequate skills in the relevant language and in the foreign legal system. this could be achieved, for example, by creating databases of legal practitioners with these skills, if they do not already exist. in my view, in order to improve the levels of competence, member states could also consider designating a single authority responsible for transmission and reception for each jurisdiction, thus ensuring that the officials responsible for these cases have sufficient experience. taking this into account, and the fact that it may be easier for the authorities of the member state of residence to communicate with the applicant and assess his financial situation, this procedure would make the action to be taken considerably easier for citizens (and also for the relevant authorities) and would make the process faster. the commission should therefore be asked to submit a proposal to amend the directive along the lines set out above.

in writing. − the over-exploitation of marine resources is a matter of concern to citizens who are aware of the need for sustainable and balanced management of ecosystems in order to ensure the survival of the human species. the report we have just voted on by mrs diane dodds concerns the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council regulation (ec) no 1342/2008 of 18 december 2008 establishing a long-term plan for cod stocks and the fisheries exploiting those stocks. over the last few decades, we have seen a reduction in some cod stocks that urgently need to be recovered. three years after the entry into force of regulation no 1342/2008, the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries carried out an evaluation of the multiannual plans for cod in the irish sea, kattegat, north sea and west of scotland and concluded that the results despite the short timeframe had fallen short of expectations. i voted in favour of this proposal because it aims to strengthen and increase cooperation between fishermen and scientists in order to reduce catches with a view to replenishing stocks and by using other areas or fishing gear without jeopardising fishermen's jobs.
in writing. − the long-term plan for cod stocks and the fisheries exploiting those stocks (regulation no 1342/2008) was an effort to recover cod stocks in northern waters. three years after it was introduced, it was reviewed by the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries (stecf), which published its assessment of the multiannual plans for cod (irish sea, kattegat, and north sea, west of scotland). recognising that it is premature to draw conclusions on the medium-term impact of the plan, stecf considered that the plan did not provide for a reduction in fishing mortality rates. it also pointed out that it did not benefit from the support of the interested parties. however, a plan that has the support of the stakeholders has a better chance of success, since actions by the fisheries sector are essential to its success. the amendments proposed by the rapporteur aim to strengthen and increase cooperation between scientists specialising in fisheries and the sector, taking as a starting point cases of successful projects in various fisheries, which have already been observed. the objective is to reduce cod catches and discards and to enable sustainable catches of other target species. we voted in favour.
in writing. − some problems have arisen in the application of this directive. as different methodologies have been applied to calculate fishing effort, when setting national reference values and when calculating the annual use of effort, certain member states have benefited from higher levels of fishing effort than those provided for in the plan. this amendment clarifies that, although there are different calculation methods, member states should use, for the calculation of the annual utilisation of their effort, a method identical to that applied when setting their national reference values for effort. the proposed amendment is therefore necessary to ensure that the plan works as intended. this will allow for better management of cod stocks and their long-term sustainability. all member states are thus on an equal footing.
in writing. − the aim of this report was to amend regulation (ec) no 1342/2008 establishing a long-term plan for cod stocks and the fisheries exploiting those stocks, on the basis of an assessment and a recovery plan for fisheries resources drawn up by the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries (stecf). in this context, the amendments made to the commission proposal are aimed at achieving the priority objective of the recovery of cod stocks, taking due account of the views of the scientific community and promoting a desirable cooperation between the sector and fisheries researchers. the amendments proposed in the report are essentially aimed at reducing cod catches by retaining sustainable catches of target species and reducing by-catch discards. to this end, measures at area and gear level, an improvement in the method of calculating by-catches in mixed fisheries and the introduction of some flexibility in the control of fishing effort when selective gear is used and approved by the stecf are suggested. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the measures proposed for this long-term management plan contribute to a balanced and sustainable exploitation of cod stocks.
in writing. − the purpose of this proposal is to amend regulation (ec) no 1342/2008 establishing a long-term plan for cod stocks and the fisheries exploiting those stocks, in the light of the evaluation of the plan drawn up by the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries (stecf). the main legal action aims to improve and clarify as far as possible the provisions of regulation (ec) no 1342/2008 identified as problematic in the evaluation. the rapporteur believes that such a change in the plan for cod stocks depends on the strengthening of cooperation between fisheries scientists and the sector, and that only then will it be possible to make a fruitful effort to restore cod stocks in the north sea waters of the european union. i voted in favour of the development of a new long-term plan for cod stocks, which would strike the right balance between keeping fishing rates at levels acceptable to the sector and properly reconstituting fish stocks.
in writing. the aim of the commission proposal is to establish a long-term plan for cod stocks and the fisheries exploiting those stocks, taking into account the evaluation of the plan by the scientific committee. the main measure of the proposal is to improve and clarify, as far as possible, the provisions of the regulation which are considered problematic. parliament has therefore moved forward with some amendments with a view to a long-term plan. i therefore voted in favour of the document.
in writing. - i approve this report, taking into account that corruption, money laundering and organised crime represent a threat to european democracy and its citizens, as well as to legal markets. in a time of economic and social crisis, all resources diverted from legal activities must be recovered and directed to the real economy, supporting legal work.
in writing. − criminal organisations have been expanding their spheres of influence, taking advantage of the new opportunities offered by the absence of controls at the eu's internal borders, economic globalisation and technological progress. they have a new corporate face, taking advantage of the considerable financial resources accumulated through their illicit activities, posing a real threat to the security and prosperity of citizens. although the eu has adopted several legal instruments with the aim of effectively combating transnational organised crime, there are still huge differences between member states, which call into question their effectiveness, and therefore it is necessary to ensure greater harmonisation and coordination between them. money laundering is linked not only to the typical activities of organised crime but also to corruption and tax crimes. in order to combat this effectively, a coherent and homogeneous legislative framework should be established, providing for proportionate and dissuasive sanctions and reinforcing judicial and police cooperation at european and international level. the fight against corruption in the public and private sectors must also be placed at the top of the political agenda, under the dual heading of repression and prevention, by strengthening the rules on incompatibilities, transparency, control of financing and the raising of funds.
in writing. − organized crime has taken advantage of the new opportunities brought by economic globalisation and technological progress and has become a transnational and global phenomenon with devastating economic and social effects. moreover, organised crime, corruption and money laundering, although still distinct phenomena, are now in many cases intertwined. the new sophisticated forms of organised crime, corruption and money laundering require effective and strong measures, and the globalisation of criminal networks also requires a global and joint eu response, and here is an important contribution to that end.
in writing. - organized crime, corruption and money laundering are a global scourge of very complex contours which must be tackled. the fight against this parallel economy, which escapes the fiscal control of the states and feeds an often well-organized underworld, is only possible through intensive cross-border cooperation. at eu level, it is estimated that more than €120 billion, which could and should contribute to economic growth and job creation, is not being controlled by the authorities. corruption, illegal betting on sports competitions, online gaming and tobacco trafficking are just a few examples of untaxed activities that deserve greater attention from cross-border investigation teams such as europol and eurojust. i voted in favour of the interim report by mr salvatore iacolino on organized crime, corruption and money laundering: recommendations on measures and initiatives to be developed, because i am in favour of the practice of an honest and responsible policy which puts an end to these shameful systems which harm all european taxpayers. we have an obligation to make european society fairer and safer by protecting citizens and returning money to public coffers.
in writing. − the report addresses relevant issues and contains some positive recommendations. however, the whole dimension of the prevention of organised crime, corruption and money laundering is grossly neglected. the repressive dimension prevails, not so much the necessary fight against the source of these phenomena. the report suggests that offshore and tax havens - a key element in money laundering - should be listed, whereas the urgent need is to dismantle them. nothing is said about the effects of the free movement of capital on the phenomena of corruption, organised crime and money laundering. the report unintentionally advances support for the so-called banking union, which, in addition to being a way of promoting concentration and centralisation of the sector, could be a way for banks to escape the regulatory and legislative control of political power. the fight against these phenomena must not ignore the fact that their results are all the more effective the closer they are to the reality in which they occur. the fact that the national structures responsible for combating these phenomena have been drained and weakened is a serious setback in this fight, which no supranational structure can replace.
in writing. - organized crime is becoming more and more worrying and is no longer a geographically limited phenomenon. increasingly, the traditional mafia-like organisations that exist in certain regions of southern europe have gradually widened their spheres of influence, taking advantage of the new opportunities offered by economic globalisation and technological progress, by forming alliances with criminal groups in other countries, and even on other continents, all within the framework of numerous criminal activities and profit opportunities. in this way, the influence on local economies, societies and institutions is an increasingly tangible phenomenon at all latitudes. this type of crime is now a global economic entity that operates on the basis of enormous illicit competitive advantages and fraudulently disrupts the legal economy. the use of new technologies and the prerogatives offered by the lisbon treaty will make it possible to combat this phenomenon less unequally and more effectively.
in writing. − organized crime is now a global economic entity that operates on the basis of enormous illicit competitive advantages and fraudulently disrupts the legal economy. i voted in favour of this interim report of the special committee on organised crime, corruption and money laundering, which calls for the creation of a european public prosecutor's office, as proposed in article 86 tfeu, in particular to combat, investigate, prosecute and bring to justice crimes against the financial interests of the european union, as well as serious cross-border crime.
in writing. the report focuses on identifying priorities for the development of a roadmap for effectively combating crime in europe and worldwide. the report also calls for the eu to take action to combat terrorism and to ensure that the eu's external borders are not encroached upon by terrorists. this is a global challenge and as such it requires a global response: the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules. the report also calls for the eu to take action to combat terrorism and to ensure that the eu is able to take action to combat terrorism. i have to say that i am not in favour of the commission's proposal to introduce a new system of penalties for the use of drugs, but i am in favour of the commission's proposal to introduce a new system of penalties for the use of drugs.
in writing. − organized crime is a global problem which must also be tackled at world level. for these reasons, this own-initiative report presents a set of contributions with a view to creating a european response to this global problem. corruption and money laundering are often associated with organised crime. the union has had a special committee on organised crime, corruption and money laundering since 2012, which, through meetings between academics, ngos, member states and european decision-makers, aims to create more effective european and national legislation. this requires strengthening judicial and police cooperation at european and international level and providing for the use of new technologies in the fight against cybercrime. this report sets out a set of guidelines which should be taken into account in the fight against organised crime.
in writing. - despite some positive aspects in this report, the general approach is to repress rather than combat it at its source as would be necessary. the majority of the ep does not exercise the necessary self-criticism of its responsibilities in this area, nor does the eu as a whole. on the contrary, it takes advantage of this report to move forward with further harmonisation of matters which are and should remain at the heart of the national sovereignty of the member states over their justice systems, such as the proposal to set up a criminal investigation body and an internal investigation agency, a mechanism to monitor the effectiveness of criminal justice systems and a european public prosecutor's office. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the taxation of capital. nothing is said about the need to put an end to the free movement of capital and the phenomena of corruption, organised crime and money laundering which continue to flourish in this way. and the so-called banking union is supported, which, in addition to being a way of promoting concentration and centralisation of the sector, will be a useful way for banks to escape the regulatory and legislative control of political power.
in writing. - i approve this report, considering first of all that social housing is a right. it is not a cost, but a reproductive investment with broad positive impacts on society and the economy. the crisis should not be used as an excuse to cut spending on social housing, especially when the demand for housing is increasing. it is necessary to ensure that adequate funds are available for social housing purposes and to ensure consistency between the various european union policies in this area, including state aid, competition policy and the structural funds.
in writing. − in portugal, between 2009 and 2011, there was an increase of around 2000 social housing fires, reaching 119 000 fires. for every 100,000 people, there are 1,123 social housing fires. in the european union, more than 25 million people live in social housing. this report, although it deals with a subject of great importance for the member states of the european union, especially in the context of the crisis we are experiencing, went beyond its competence. national and local authorities have, and should continue to have, competences in formulating and implementing social housing policies adapted to the context of each member state. i therefore abstained in the final vote on this report, because i believe that the principle of subsidiarity applies to this matter.
in writing. − access to housing is a fundamental right, which can be seen as a precondition both for the exercise of other fundamental rights and for a human life in full dignity. it is up to the member states to define their social housing policy and to take the necessary measures to safeguard this right by allowing their citizens to have access to decent and affordable housing. the deep long-term economic and social impact of the crisis, in terms of economic growth, employment rates and levels of poverty and social exclusion (with 120 million europeans already living in or at risk of poverty), makes it necessary and urgent that member states, despite the differences between them, step up their efforts to address the growing need for affordable housing and to ensure access to decent housing for their citizens. the eu should support this effort by encouraging investment in social housing, notably through the use of the structural funds, for which a sufficient allocation should be ensured under the next multiannual financial framework.
in writing. - in portugal, in recent decades, much has been done to ensure that the most disadvantaged and those at risk of social exclusion can exercise their right to housing and have a right to a decent life. however, in view of the current economic situation and the fact that a number of member states, particularly those on the periphery, are implementing difficult fiscal consolidation measures and structural reforms, i believe that the role of the state should be to encourage competition in the real estate sector and to push for good legislation. in this connection, i would like to recall the recent legislative measures taken in portugal to make the leasing market more flexible.
in writing. - article 34 (3) of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union states that in order to combat social exclusion and poverty, the union recognises and respects the right to social assistance and housing assistance to ensure a decent existence for all those who lack sufficient resources, in accordance with community law and national laws and practices. the economic and financial crisis we are going through has made it difficult to realize the right to decent housing universally recognized by all states. increasing unemployment, wage cuts and cuts in social benefits make it increasingly difficult to achieve this right. i therefore call on the european central bank to facilitate the building credit that can stimulate economic growth and job creation. because social housing cannot be considered an expense but an investment, i voted in favour of the report on social housing in the european union by my colleague karima delli and i call on the eu institutions to support the member states in their policies to support social housing, thus contributing to the achievement of the europe 2020 objectives of reducing poverty, social exclusion and combating climate change.
in writing. - the so-called austerity policies imposed by the imf/eu and national governments have led to an increase in social inequalities, unemployment, poverty and the population at risk of poverty. more and more people and families are being denied the right to housing. against this background, investment in the social housing sector is an urgent social need. we appreciate that several of our proposed amendments to the report have been accepted, which has greatly improved the final version. unfortunately, formulations have also been adopted which place the policy of social housing within the euro plus pact and the so-called economic and budgetary governance of the european union, policies which have precisely conditioned public investment, destroyed public services and social rights which the report says it wants to defend.
in writing. − this report aims to show how the social housing sector can be a lever to help the european union emerge from the economic, social and environmental crisis. some 25 million european citizens live in social housing. all member states except greece have a social housing stock, the size of which varies widely between member states, particularly between the western member states and the newest ones in the east. social housing needs also vary within a member state, between urban and rural areas, and even within urban areas, between city centres and their peripheries. social housing is one of the possible responses of public authorities to the inability of the housing market to meet all housing needs and to ensure access to decent housing at an affordable price/income for all. that is why i am voting in favour.
in writing. - it is estimated that 25 million citizens of the european union live in social housing. all member states except greece have social housing, although the size of the whole varies from one country to another. social housing is an instrument through which the authorities can provide adequate housing at affordable rents to certain segments of the population, as the private housing market is unable to meet the demand of low-income households. investing in social housing not only has a beneficial effect on the construction sector, but also reduces the risk of real estate or rental bubbles bursting. social housing, in addition to ensuring access to affordable, decent housing, also has a beneficial effect on other socially challenged areas. considering that social housing plays a key role in the implementation of key european policies, as it contributes to ensuring high levels of employment, social inclusion and cohesion, while promoting mobility and even combating energy poverty through its contribution to the modernisation of the housing stock, i supported this report which calls on the member states to establish and organise a parallel supply of social housing to complement the supply generated by private initiative.
in writing. − social housing plays an important role in european societies. currently, an estimated 25 million people live in social housing, a situation that could increase as the sovereignty crisis continues. in addition, social housing protects those considered to be most vulnerable, including the elderly, marginalised groups, young people and children and their dependants. although i believe that social housing can reduce discrimination and promote the well-being of those sections of society who do not find adequate supply in the market, i believe that each member state should have discretion to apply measures, the so-called principle of subsidiarity. for these reasons, i abstain from this report.

in writing. - in the 1960s, as is the case with many young people today, thousands upon thousands of portuguese left their homeland in search of another country where they could secure their livelihood and that of their families. the men left in search of work, while their wives, mostly domestic workers, stayed behind to care for the home and the children. because of the husband's departure abroad, many became known as black widows for walking around in black. these women, because of their low professional and academic qualifications, had great difficulty in finding employment, except in agricultural work. the new generation of women is now more qualified than the male generation, and the new wave of youth emigration, besides being the most qualified ever, is certainly the one that includes the largest number of women. since 2007, the erasmus programme has been promoting and supporting student mobility. of the approximately 3 million people who have benefited from this support, 60% are women. i voted in favour of the report on the educational and professional mobility of women in the european union because it is necessary to support and encourage their mobility if we are to achieve the objectives set by the europe 2020 strategy of having 75% of the female employed population by 2020.

in writing. - mr jim higgins reports to us on a strategy for an electronic toll service and a vignette system for light private vehicles. the use of road infrastructure raises a number of problems which need to be solved. of course, we need to get funding for its conservation. it is absurd to require those who do not use the motorways to contribute to their maintenance. i therefore support the principle of user/payer. another issue addressed in this report concerns the method of charging for use. as far as possible, there should be harmonisation in order to facilitate movement throughout the european union (eu). the tolling identifier acquired by a citizen of any member state should be recognised on all eu motorways. by ending the queues at toll booths, we would be contributing to the improvement of the economy and to the fight against climate change. i voted in favour of this report because i agree with the need for self-financing of road structures and the adoption of a system which not only brings environmental benefits but also improves access to european markets.
in writing. the report aims to establish a strategy for a european-wide electronic toll service and a vignette system for private light vehicles in europe. at the heart of the argument is the principle of user-payer/polluter-payer as a key priority for the transport sector. the absolute application of this principle, which we disagree with, ignores the fact that, as we had the opportunity to say during the debate in plenary, road infrastructure responds to economic and social needs which cannot be dissociated from a specific regional and territorial context. these specificities must obviously weigh on the type of operation and functioning of each infrastructure, including whether or not tolls are introduced and who is or is not liable to pay them. the experience of the introduction of tolls in the scut in portugal reflects the disastrous results of the strict application of the above principles. we are not opposed to measures which facilitate car travel between the different european countries, in the context of safeguarding the right to a public, rational and high-quality road network. but this is not the view of this report, which does not address the concerns we have expressed, but instead advocates a harmonization of the service, imposing its adoption by the member states with sanctioning measures for cases of non-application or non-compliance.
in writing. - seep was a complete failure, so the commission should present as soon as possible a new proposal for a regulation to ensure that seep becomes a reality. we must therefore work together to have an effective seep. the use of online payment systems is essential to ensure price transparency as well as convenience, in particular for users not resident in the member state where the fee is charged.
in writing. - it is not too much to underline the importance of the higgins report on the electronic road toll system. the importance of the user-pays principle - and hence the collection of tolls - in the financing of road infrastructure should be emphasised. moreover, in an integrated economy based on freedom of movement, a mechanism for the interoperability of national electronic toll systems is essential. the current european electronic toll service (eets) established by the union is not being implemented and binding legislative measures for the operationalisation of that service are urgently needed, taking into account the technical solutions currently available. european citizens and businesses cannot continue to be victims of the unwillingness of some member states to ensure effective freedom of movement on the roads throughout the union. if there are two essential measures to ensure that european citizens have a sense of european integration, they are the abolition of roaming in telephone services and the effective introduction of an interoperable electronic toll service at union level.
