in writing. − in view of the current socioeconomic situation, which is particularly difficult in the peripheral member states, i welcome the recent commission communication entitled 'social investment for growth and cohesion, including through the european social fund, for the period 2014-2020. the european union currently has 10.5% of unemployed, 22.8% of young people, 27% of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion and a 15% drop-out rate. these are values which i consider absolutely untenable today and which call into question our rule of law. it is therefore of the utmost importance that the european union acts swiftly and establishes the proper link between national social policies, the european semester reform process and the relevant eu cohesion funds.
in writing. the resolution welcomes the commission's proposal on the social investment package and presents it as the future solution to the crisis. this package, it is said, will promote economic growth and job creation. while social investment can play a central role in strengthening social cohesion, social inclusion and the fight against poverty and social exclusion, it will certainly not do so in the way now proposed by the european commission (which this resolution welcomes and supports). the resolution welcomes the fact that the social investment package promotes public-private partnerships and project obligations. it also encourages the mobility of workers and defends the principles of flexicurity. this package is inseparable from the european semester, the euro plus pact and the so-called economic governance, instruments which synthesise a path of strongly conditioning public investment, of the destruction and privatisation of public services, of the attack on social rights and of the increase in exploitation, with the reduction of unit labour costs and the weight of wages in national income. we voted against it, of course.
in writing. − in several member states, fiscal consolidation measures have led to the promotion of short-term expenditure objectives at the expense of investment in sustainable growth, employment, social cohesion and competitiveness. on the other hand, the sovereign debt crisis that has hit europe, in particular the euro area countries, has led to a sharp economic slowdown with negative social consequences in most member states through increased unemployment, poverty levels and social exclusion. the crisis has highlighted the economic interdependence of member states and the significant differences in the ability of individual member states to respond to labour market and social challenges. so we all have to make an extra effort to make social investment for growth and cohesion a reality. i believe that this investment will make a decisive contribution to the solution of this crisis.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution on the commission communication entitled 'social investment for growth and cohesion, including through the european social fund, 2014-2020. i agree with most of the statements made, particularly where it is stressed that social investment should be seen as an investment by the member states that can provide a long-term return even in a counter-cyclical situation. i also agree with the request to the commission to examine what part of public social expenditure can be considered as productive investment.
in writing. − sustainable growth, employment, social cohesion and competitiveness have been severely hampered by the fiscal consolidation measures implemented in the wake of the public debt crisis, which required short-term spending cuts. the effects of economic stagnation are challenging social protection and social security systems, since without growth there is no employment and without employment there is a deepening of poverty, which, together with budget cuts in public services and budgets and social assistance, leads to conditions of severe material deprivation. it is essential that citizens can find decent employment and an opportunity to live in dignity. this report thus looks at the eu funds, whose chain of command can and should contribute to strengthening the union's social dimension through growth-enhancing social investment, towards sustainable and inclusive reform. i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution.
in writing. − at a time of high economic and social difficulties, job creation must be placed at the centre of the european institutions and the member states' attention. it should be noted that 27% of children are at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 8% of eu citizens live in conditions of severe material deprivation and cannot access the necessities considered essential to live a dignified life in europe, and 15% of children leave school without completing secondary education. i am voting in favour of this resolution which calls for job creation and contributes to specific solutions to combat the unemployment which exists throughout the european union, especially among young people, which has now reached six million.
in writing. the commission's proposal on the social investment package is hailed as the future solution to the crisis. the advocates of this say it will promote economic growth and job creation. the truth is that social investment plays a central role in strengthening social cohesion, social inclusion and the fight against poverty and social exclusion. but not in the way the commission proposes. the resolution welcomes the fact that the social investment package promotes public-private partnerships and project obligations, encourages worker mobility and defends the principles of flexicurity. this package is linked to the european semester and is based on european economic governance, structural policies which have precisely conditioned public investment, destroyed public services, jobs and social rights.
in writing. - i approve this report, considering that regional aid can only be effective if it is used in a moderate and proportionate way and concentrated in the most disadvantaged regions of the eu, where it is needed most. i therefore believe that state aid policy and cohesion policy are largely complementary and mutually reinforcing. in this respect, i urge the commission to ensure that the modernisation of state aid is consistent with the proposed amendments to the general regulation on the structural funds and to avoid that regions belonging to the same category and facing similar economic difficulties are treated differently. i would also stress the structural contribution of aid to regional development, especially in the current context of a serious economic crisis, and i would therefore ask the commission to recognise that the criterion for defining a crisis, which specifies a serious disturbance in the economy of a member state, continued to apply in the real economy as well as in the financial sector.
in writing. − the existence of less developed regions in the european union and the fact that some regions face specific problems arising from their ultraperiphery make it advisable for regional incentives to play a relevant role in the support provided by the european union. economic growth in the union requires that the specific circumstances of the regions for which support is intended be taken into account and that the regions be able to take account of their reality. complementarity between cohesion policy and state aid is crucial in order to get the best out of both.
in writing. - this report deals with an old question - a question of the matrix of the process of european capitalist integration. the eu largely restricts and prevents state intervention in the economy. it affects the way in which each member state, taking account of its specific situation and the needs of its regions, plans and allocates so-called state aid. it thus calls into question a democratic intervention of the state in the economy. it is therefore calling democracy itself into question by excluding this possibility of intervention. and it does so to open the door to market dictatorship. but these limitations never call into question the channelling of generous public resources to large private groups, some multinationals, which shortly after receiving large amounts of public funding move to other countries, robbing more public support and leaving a trail of destruction and unemployment wherever they go. we also regret that the obligation for these companies to remain in the country where they receive aid has not been extended for at least ten years, instead of the current five. the rules referred to in the report are particularly damaging to the most disadvantaged regions, limiting their development. we voted against it.
in writing. − the commission is pursuing the process of modernising state aid, the objectives of which are to promote growth and focus on the most important cases, and to simplify, streamline and accelerate the application of the relevant rules. i agree that the draft regional aid guidelines (rag) for 2014-2020 are an integral part of the modernisation programme of the eu's state aid policy (sap) and with the adoption of simpler, more predictable and effective state aid control and enforcement rules, based on sound economic analysis. that is why i am voting in favour.
in writing. − the european commission launched the debate on the legislative package on cohesion policy in june 2011. the objective is to contribute to a more competitive european union and to the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, in particular through investment in the context of cohesion policy, while helping the least developed regions to develop on an equal footing with the most developed regions. i voted in favour of this report which presents solutions which are beneficial for the outermost regions.
in writing. - i consider that state aid to the most disadvantaged regions with special and permanent characteristics, such as the outermost regions, is an essential instrument for promoting their development. in fact, a specific derogating regime from the prohibition on state aid to the outermost regions is enshrined in the treaty. it also respects the achievement of the objective of territorial cohesion by taking into account regional specificities and by being adapted to those specificities. but such a system must be simple and flexible, or else it will become ineffective and lose some of the positive effects that have been produced over the years in these regions. for the reasons i have given, i voted in favour of the document.
in writing. - i approve this report, considering that we are now in the fifth year of the financial, economic and social crisis. competition has proved to be a necessary tool in responding to crises. it has stopped protectionist and market-fragmenting trends, provided a framework of guidelines that has contributed to financial stability and restructuring, and fostered fairer competition in more transparent financial markets. during these years, competition policy was the only tool for resolving the banking crisis at european level and the experience gained by the commission should be useful in the progress towards a banking union. at the same time, it has helped member states to maximise the effectiveness of public intervention. competition is always important and essential in difficult times. in my view, the greatest ally for economic reconstruction is competition policy. antitrust, state aid and merger control all have a direct impact on the drivers of productivity and competitiveness. strong competition is necessary to meet the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth.
in writing. − this european parliament report reflects on the competition policies implemented by the european commission in 2011 with the aim of promoting the competitiveness of the european economy and achieving the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. the importance of antitrust, state aid and merger policies is emphasised in order to foster a healthy competition policy which is beneficial for european citizens. the need to promote actions to facilitate the protection of businesses and consumers harmed by the failures of european regulation, to make competition policy more legitimate through greater involvement of the european parliament, to ensure that state aid functions as temporary measures and does not drag on over time, to supervise the activity of large business conglomerates and public services and to ensure the proper functioning of the european food sector is emphasised. competition policy must be preserved as it is one of the fundamental instruments for ensuring the dynamic and transparent functioning of markets, prevents fragmentation and protectionism and is vital in the fight against the economic crisis. i support this report because it contributes to the preservation of an open, fair and active european market, and ensures a higher quality of services for citizens.

in writing. − competition policy is part of the eu's dna. the treaty of rome created the three instruments of competition policy (antitrust, state aid and merger control) which aim to preserve equality and an open and dynamic market. free competition helps companies to seek success through their merits based on prices, quality and innovation satisfying the needs, preferences and desires of intermediaries and final consumers. i consider the commission's report on competition policy 2011 to be very important and welcome the fact that the new thematic structure addresses the issues highlighted by parliament and allows for a clear identification of priorities, objectives and actions undertaken.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the annual report on competition policy by mr sánchez presedo, which gives a good account of the situation and problems of competition policy in the european union. since the beginning of european economic integration with the treaty of rome in 1957, the economic order of the union has been based on an orderly market economy, including the active defence of competition against restrictive practices and abuses of dominant positions by undertakings and against state aid liable to distort competition. in this connection, the report suggests that the state aid regime should be made more flexible, given the economic crisis in the union. in addition, since the 1986-92 internal market programme, the union has been actively promoting the opening up of former public utilities (electricity, telecommunications, transport, etc.) to competition, without prejudice to the guarantee of public service obligations. in this respect, the report takes note of the backlog of the single market in energy and rail transport and the need for consistency in the regulation of services of general interest (sgeis) as required by the eu treaties.

in writing. − according to the latest statistics available from eurostat, in march 2013 the youth unemployment rate (i.e. workers under the age of 25) in the european union was 23.5%, corresponding to 5.7 million young people without a job, and 24% in the euro area, corresponding to 3.6 million unemployed. this social scourge has been increasing over the last few months, as a year-on-year comparison (to march 2012) shows that the youth unemployment figures have been rising considerably, with more than 170 000 young people now without a job. new measures to combat youth unemployment are urgently needed and the european institutions must involve the political youth organisations and youth associations that face this problem on a daily basis.
in writing. - i approve this report, beginning with my reiteration of my efforts to revise regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, which should, in a global way, enable eu citizens to have greater and better access to eu documents. the commission is thus called upon to commit fully, at political and technical level, to amending and adapting regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 to the provisions of the lisbon treaty, or to take appropriate measures to overcome the impasse. at the same time, the council was instructed to resume its discussions on regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 as soon as possible, to adopt its position at first reading and to continue negotiations. i end by reiterating its position at first reading, adopted on 15 december 2011, as the starting point for negotiations, and insist that an amended text, as a minimum condition and in conformity with the requirements of the treaty, should: explicitly extend the scope of application to all institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the european union, strengthen legislative transparency, including access to legal opinions on legislative matters.
in writing. - there are commonplace things that seem right but are just that. the idea that there can never be too much transparency sounds good, but in practice it is not true. simplicity often results in simplicity which is detrimental to all. in addition to transparency, there are other values which deserve protection and which must be taken into account. there are duties of confidentiality and data protection that are not compatible with unjustified absolutisms that are better suited to more basic decision-making levels and methods than those employed in the european union. more than commonplaces, common sense is required.
in writing. - transparency is the essence of democracy and must be at its service. the eu, as an example of how democracy works, felt the need to show its citizens that it had nothing to hide and that is why 12 years ago it adopted its first transparency regulation. access to information and documents of public bodies is a fundamental right of citizens and should be treated as such. however, a certain degree of confidentiality is necessary in certain matters, both for personal and copyright reasons and to prevent misuse by those who may have privileged access to certain information. on 20 april 2008, the commission presented a proposal for a recast of regulation no 1049/2001 of the european parliament and of the council of 30 may 2011 regarding public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. an improved proposal was subsequently submitted, although complementary to the first, which was to be adopted by this parliament in december 2011. the council has not yet adopted the regulation, a year and a half later, and this is putting the credibility of the european institutions in doubt. because the violation of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which enshrines the right to information, is at issue, i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.
in writing. − regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 governs public access to documents of the eu institutions the european parliament, the council and the commission. the lack of transparency is evident in the council working groups and trilogues, the publication of legal opinions on legislative processes, the work of eu agencies, international negotiations and the commission's dialogue with member states. however, the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon has increased the european union's obligations in the field of transparency and has enshrined access to documents as a fundamental right, and therefore that regulation needs to be reviewed. it is not therefore understood that the revision of this regulation is at an impasse under the responsibility of the commission and the council. the resolution considers that the amendment of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 should be a priority for all eu institutions. we support the need to deepen transparency at all levels in the european union. but we regret that several exceptions to public access to documents remain.
in writing. - i believe that transparency is an essential tool to enable citizens to participate in the decision-making process of the european union, and to ensure that the european institutions are accountable to citizens and thus strengthen their commitment and confidence. in this sense, the entry into force of the lisbon treaty has reinforced the european union's obligations in the field of transparency and enshrined access to documents as a fundamental right. i therefore think it is important that an agreed platform be found to give all eu citizens access to documents.
in writing. − transparency is an essential tool to enable citizens to participate in the decision-making process of the european union, and to ensure that the european institutions are accountable to citizens and thus strengthen their commitment and confidence. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution, which calls for the full application of the regulation on public access to european parliament, council and commission documents.
in writing. − regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 is seen by eu citizens as a key piece of legislation that provides the tools for the proper monitoring of eu actions. however, the various cases handled by the ombudsman show that the application of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 still needs improvement. the commission has proposed a recast of the regulation to improve the criteria for the accountability of the european institutions to their citizens and thus increase their involvement and trust. but the negotiations are deadlocked. considering that failure to agree on a new version of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 would send the wrong signal to eu citizens and considering further that a failure to negotiate could undermine the legitimacy of the decision-making process, i voted in favour of this resolution, which calls on the council to immediately resume discussions on regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 and to adopt its position at first reading and proceed immediately with the negotiations.
in writing. − the lisbon treaty has emphasised the european union's obligations in the field of transparency and enshrined access to documents as a fundamental right of all citizens. the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amends regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 regarding public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. however, the cypriot and irish presidencies were unable to unblock the issue in the council and start new negotiations because of the resistance of the commission. i therefore support this report, which aims to raise awareness among the european institutions of the need to resolve this political impasse.
in writing. - regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 governs public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. there is a lack of transparency in council working groups and trilogues, in the publication of legal opinions on legislative procedures, in eu agencies, in international negotiations and in the commission's dialogue with member states. the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon has also reinforced the european union's obligations in the field of transparency and has enshrined access to documents as a fundamental right, which requires a revision of the regulation. it is not understood, therefore, that the review is at an impasse under the responsibility of the commission and the council. the resolution considers that the amendment of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 should be a priority for all eu institutions. we support the need to increase transparency at all levels of the european union, but we regret that a number of exceptions to public access to documents remain.
mr president, the protests in istanbul and other cities in turkey show that many in that country have lost patience with prime minister erdogan's authoritarian and repressive style, sadly evidenced in his reaction to peaceful protesters against the destruction of gezi park. as president gül has rightly said, democracy is more than elections. democracies do not attack protesters, do not bulldoze citizen protests or arrest journalists, and turkey is, shamefully, as has been said here today, the world's largest jailer of journalists. it was not by chance that what ignited the protests and spread them to other cities was the indignation of citizens at national radio and television stations silencing what the international media projected from taksim square to the world. the european union, which is not only a strategic partner of turkey but also has a strategic intention to accept it as a member, must unequivocally condemn the violence and the inflammatory statements and police reprisals by the prime minister and members of his government. the call for restraint between the two sides is inappropriate, both from the european union and as a message to be conveyed to a country which is a candidate for european union membership. i therefore wish to express my full support for the statements made by commissioner füle in turkey in support of democracy and human rights and for his initiative to visit taksim square. the european union cannot now simply encourage dialogue. it is essential to demand that the turkish authorities learn from these clashes and stop forcing the religious subordination of the different lifestyles in turkish society, stop persecuting journalists and activists for freedom and human rights. the turkish government has the opportunity to correct its hand. it must focus on giving institutional, legal and political space to a democratic society, respectful of transparency, accountability, and religious and political pluralism. this also requires, as has already been said here, an organized democratic opposition which responds to the aspirations of the progressive segments of turkish society. we can help by opening the crucial chapters 23 and 24 to negotiation and by making the vibrant voice of turkish society, which has put taksim square and gezi park on the world map, heard in these negotiations.

in writing. − after several years of work and thanks to the efforts of rapporteur ivailo kalfin, we have just adopted the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament (ep) and of the council amending directive 2003/98/ec on the re-use of public sector information (rist). the public sector is the largest database in existence and its knowledge can influence the markets themselves and have a major effect on transparency. the european union (eu) was therefore obliged to regulate this matter in order to avoid abuses in its handling, in particular the existence of monopolies that condition the accessibility of them. without the necessary protection of personal data, we will all have to benefit from this transparency and openness, the only way to move forward into the future and create more jobs. knowledge is the basis of the new information society. i voted in favour because public data will be more accessible to businesses and citizens under the following conditions: information generally accessible but with respect for the rules and principles of its use. i welcome the promotion of europe's cultural heritage through the opening up of data relating to museums, archives and libraries. all citizens in general and researchers in particular will have a huge data set at their fingertips.
in writing. − directive 2003/98/ec of the european parliament and of the council on the re-use of public sector information (pib directive) was adopted on 17 november 2003. the directive aimed to facilitate the re-use of public sector information across the union by harmonising the basic conditions for re-use and removing the main obstacles to re-use in the internal market. the directive includes provisions on non-discrimination, pricing, exclusive agreements, transparency, licensing and practical means to facilitate the discovery and re-use of public documents. the benefits of better access and easier reuse include: innovation in products directly based on isps and complementary products, lower costs of operations and greater efficiency in the public sector, and increasingly, the combination of different public and private information for the creation of new products.
in writing. the proposal for a directive calls for a paradigm shift towards a policy of open access to public data in the digital age. the basic principle is that the general public has a right to access data which, in the public service, is collected with funds from tax revenues. the directive includes provisions on non-discrimination, pricing, exclusive agreements, transparency, licences and practical means to facilitate the discovery and re-use of public documents, and has received further amendments from the european parliament to make it a balanced instrument and not to introduce a bureaucratic burden on public institutions. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − the european commission has presented a proposal for a directive amending directive 2003/98/ec on the reuse of public sector information. i am voting in favour of this report because i believe that the reuse of public sector information should be facilitated throughout the union by harmonising the basic conditions for reuse and by removing the main obstacles to reuse in the internal market. i would also stress that the directive includes provisions on non-discrimination, pricing, exclusive agreements, transparency, licences and practical means to facilitate the discovery and re-use of public documents.
in writing. − some of the issues raised in the report and in the directive are of concern to us, such as the protection of personal data and respect for individual freedoms and guarantees, which are often poorly considered and even inadequate. the amendments now tabled to the 2003 directive on this subject strengthen the role of public-private partnerships in this process as the commercial component of the provision of the information in question, a point with which we have many reservations, once again if public resources in the form of information, data and documentation are used to make profits and satisfy private purposes. we are also concerned that private interests may restrict access to information, that the interests of private partners in the management of information may override the general interest. we cannot accept that the market and its competition laws should decide neither the prices nor the information and documents to be made available, nor that the commission should be given, as the directive states, a competence which should belong to the member states, taking into account their reality and the characteristics of their public sector. it would be good if the free software formats used were given priority in the provision of information.

in writing. - i approve this report on the grounds that freedom of religion or belief is, among all human rights, a basic and essential right which must be respected. discrimination on the basis of religion or belief persists in all areas of the world, and in numerous countries the human rights of persons belonging to certain religious communities, including religious minorities, continue to be denied. i am therefore in favour of the purpose and scope of the eu guidelines which should always be: to promote and defend freedom of religion or belief, to integrate freedom of religion or belief into eu human rights policies and actions, to develop unambiguous benchmarks, norms and standards in order to strengthen the promotion of freedom of religion or belief in the work of public officials and officials of the european union. as a final note, i would stress that the eu's external financial instruments should be used either as incentives or as deterrents (freezing of funds) with regard to freedom of religion or belief in a given country.
in writing. - freedom of religion or belief is, among all human rights, a basic and essential right which must be respected. as such, the draft guidelines should mainstream freedom of religion or belief into eu human rights policies and actions. to this end, it should develop unambiguous benchmarks, standards and standards and increase the clarity of the definitions used.
in writing. - freedom of religion or belief is a fundamental value, structuring the kind of society in which we want to live. the right to believe and not to believe must be counterbalanced by mutual respect. regardless of belief in the transcendent or non-transcendent root of the values that allow us to live in community and the idea of the person and his dignity, no one can be forced to believe or to abjure his faith. states should not persecute the religious expressions of peoples or unreasonably suppress practices and customs that are part of their traditions and cultures. to do so is to deny the very heritage of european civilization. externally, the european union must promote and defend religious freedom in third countries and place this issue at the top of its concerns regarding fundamental rights. i would like to draw particular attention to situations of persecution of christians all over the world and i regret that some phenomena of christianophobia are also occurring in the union.
in writing. - the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, based on article xviii of the universal declaration of human rights, states in article 10 (1) that: 'everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.' this right implies the freedom to change one's religion or belief and the freedom to manifest one's religion or belief, individually or collectively, in public or in private, through worship, teaching, practice and the performance of rites. despite the enshrinement of these rights, the truth is that we are witnessing serious violations of this right on the planet, especially in the arab countries, but also in europe. egypt, iraq, burma, kazakhstan (where 2 young men were accused of blasphemy and sentenced to death for burning the koran), pakistan, etc. are countries where these violations often occur. we need early warning mechanisms that bring this kind of attack on human freedom to the attention of international authorities. i voted in favour of the report on the promotion and protection of freedom of religion or belief because it is unacceptable for anyone to be persecuted because of his religion and i urge the eu to promote a code of religious freedom throughout the world.
in writing. − the eu is founded on the principle of respect for human rights and has a legal obligation, laid down in its treaties, to ensure that all eu and member state policies, without exception, as well as all international agreements, focus on human rights. dialogues between the eu, its member states and third countries must be preceded by concrete measures designed to ensure that human rights remain at the heart of eu policies. despite the crisis we are going through, we cannot forget that the defence of human rights is part of the eu's dna. in this regard, the promotion of the right to freedom of religion or belief, including theistic, non-theistic and atheistic beliefs, the right not to have a belief and the right to change one's religion or belief, constitute universal human rights and fundamental freedoms of every human being.

in writing. − in september 2000, the united nations adopted the millennium declaration, which was followed by the setting of concrete targets and a timetable to be achieved by 2015. since then, progress has been made towards the millennium development goals (mdgs), with targets to halve both extreme poverty and the proportion of people without reliable access to improved sources of drinking water. however, two years after the deadline, much remains to be done. this year the united nations will assess progress on the current mdgs and begin to look ahead to the post-2015 development framework. in this regard, the eu cannot fail to have a coordinated and coherent position on the post-2015 development framework, supporting a responsible and comprehensive post-2015 development framework, based on the principles of human rights, equality, non-discrimination, sustainability, good governance and policy coherence for development, aiming at the creation of a just and sustainable world, where every human being can exercise their rights and live in dignity and free from poverty. i therefore supported this report.
in writing. − given that the un will assess progress on the millennium development goals (mdgs) later this year and the european commission is about to adopt a communication addressing the mdgs assessment and the post-2015 development framework, it seems to me more necessary than ever to reflect on the future of mdgs and development policy. despite the considerable progress achieved on the mdgs, it is necessary to take into account the new global landscape in which poverty is reaching new dimensions, many developing countries are highly vulnerable to shocks from climate, food and demographic crises and new challenges such as high unemployment (especially among young people), lack of social protection, environmental degradation are intensifying. i therefore consider it crucial that the eu takes a common, effective and ambitious stance in the discussions on the post-2015 framework, which should be a comprehensive framework, incorporating the core issues of development and sustainability and including for this purpose not only the mdgs but also the sustainable development goals. special emphasis should be placed on disadvantaged groups such as women, children, the elderly, the disabled, thus promoting the overall well-being and desired prosperity.

in writing. − on 8 september 2000, following the united nations millennium declaration, 191 countries adopted the millennium development goals (mdgs): eradicating extreme poverty and hunger, achieving universal primary education, promoting gender equality and the empowerment of women, reducing child mortality, improving maternal health, combating hiv/aids, malaria and other diseases, ensuring environmental sustainability and creating a global partnership for development. the mdgs were intended to be achieved in a time frame of 15 years. with two years to go, it is the ideal time to take stock of what has been achieved and prepare a post-2015 framework. the mdgs have reduced poverty and hunger, access to clean water, access to education for many children, and so on. despite this success, much remains to be done to fully achieve the mdgs. i voted in favour of the report drawn up by filip kaczmarek because i agree with his recommendations that we should be optimistic and reach an agreement. despite the dwindling financial resources, we must look for alternative sources of funding so that we can continue to help the poorest to build, universally, a more just society.

the fight against road accidents must first of all recognise the multiple causes of this phenomenon, which implies action at various levels in promoting road safety. a strategy to substantially reduce the number of injuries must be based on a broad debate involving experts, the public and drivers. in the present circumstances, the analysis of this problem cannot ignore, among other factors, the impact of the deteriorated state of many roads and the state of maintenance of some vehicles. in portugal, the installation of tolls on several motorways without quality road alternatives has led to a very sharp growth in traffic on roads with lower safety conditions. the importation by some countries of heavy vehicles which have already outlived their useful life in their countries of origin and, in general, the degradation of the public transport service, the further liberalization of vehicle inspection activity, favouring business to the detriment of the certification function and worsening the working conditions of technicians, the insistence on public-private road partnerships, are factors, among many others, which cannot also be ignored in this discussion.
madam president, commissioner, water pollution is a threat to the aquatic environment, it jeopardizes the quality and quantity of drinking water and it is one of the main environmental concerns. the water directive set the objective of achieving good environmental, chemical and quantitative status of european water bodies by 2015 and defined strategies to combat pollution. the review of the list of priority substances has identified new substances which pose a risk to the aquatic environment. the agreement reached does not include the three drugs in the priority list but does include them in the watch list. the important thing is to monitor the presence of pharmaceutical substances in the water because they are hazardous to health, and being on the watch list allows us to do that monitoring and that monitoring, we hope. the progressive extension of the maximum number of substances in the watch list and the exploration of synergies with other relevant legislation such as reach or legislation on pesticides and biocides is welcome.
madam president, water is an inalienable public good. their good conservation requires the observance of stringent criteria that ensure a high level of protection of public health and the environment, but it requires more: it requires public water and outreach services, public research and development institutions, specialised technical and scientific personnel, as well as a set of firm measures to defend, secure and protect water as a strategic public good. all this is now being called into question in several countries, such as portugal, where the european commission, through an intolerable and repeated policy of interference, as it has itself admitted, has been pushing for the privatisation of water services, imposing policies and measures which seriously weaken the capacity for monitoring and intervention in defence of water, its quality and good conservation. it is a move which is in flagrant contradiction to all the rhetoric which justifies this legislation, even in view of its obvious weakening as a result of the negotiations between parliament and the council.
mr president, on 27 june a general strike was held in portugal, with one of the largest numbers ever in the whole country and in the various sectors of activity, industry, services, the private sector and the public sector. in industry, the closure of many companies, such as the alfeite arsenal, the viana do castelo shipyards or lisnave. in the fisheries sector, there was a general stoppage of fishing lots and fleets. in transport, widespread stoppage of trains and metros and national seaports and a huge impact on airport operations. in the public administration, many hospitals and health centers were hit hard by the strike. many young people with precarious ties who, despite the situation of blackmail in which they live, have had the courage to stand up for their rights. and many other examples. what are the european institutions' views on the general strike in portugal? not one. because this strike was an undeniable demand for the rejection of right-wing policies, as reflected in the agreement with the troika, that is, the policies of the european union. the portuguese workers want the troika out of portugal and they have said it loudly, exercising their right to strike. the european union is so democratic that it pretends that nothing has happened.

i congratulate mrs toia on putting on the european agenda the extraordinary capacity for performance that the cooperative sector is demonstrating in these times of crisis that we are going through. i would particularly stress its suitability and potential to generate the much needed sustainable responses in the economic, social and environmental fields which have been so badly hit. the greatest resilience of cooperative enterprises, including financial ones, is due to their model of partnerships which put the interests of all their members first, making their participation and security in the medium and long term inalienable principles. a clearly opposite model to those that focus on the pursuit of high short-term profits to serve the interests of a few and that have led us to this crisis. i therefore call for a practical and ambitious push to make the cooperative model a useful tool for jobseekers and all those trying to ensure the continuity of their businesses, so that they can find in it a valuable way of organising and financing their activity.
mr president, cooperatives are a form of economic organisation with specific characteristics, values and principles which are opposed to the logic of the private market. the socialisation of profits for the benefit of the cooperative enterprise, the principles of equality between its members, the strong economic and social link with the environment in which they are integrated, and respect for industrial relations are values which, in the context of the intensification of neoliberal policies, must be defended and supported. we are therefore in favour of this report in general. however, there is a whole framework in the report with which we disagree: the inclusion of cooperatives in the single market, which is based on the logic of competitiveness and the colonization of the weakest economies by the strongest, is diametrically opposed to the principles governing cooperatives. it would also be important to clarify that, in the process of transforming a solvent company into a cooperative, it is not the workers who inherit the debts that were not created by them, but by the private managers. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
mr president, in a context of inexorable and progressive scarcity of resources and of increasing harmful accumulation in the environment of by-products resulting from their consumption, resource efficiency and the recovery and treatment of waste are unquestionably priority areas for intensifying research and development efforts. more than a means of simply harnessing innovative ideas that can be transformed into products and services to be launched on the market, the investment effort in these areas is a necessary means of responding to the problems and challenges facing humanity today. innovation must be a key element of public policies in areas such as the environment, water, energy, agriculture, transport and others, but we must not forget that in many countries, and especially in those countries targeted by the european union and the imf, the limitation, and even the destruction, of technical and scientific capacity resulting from the so-called austerity policies irreparably compromise investment in this and other areas.
member of the commission. - mr president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr bartolozzi, for his comprehensive proposal and for parliament’s strong support for the bioeconomy strategy and action plan. we fully endorse the view that a modern, well-functioning bioeconomy is a prerequisite for achieving the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. like parliament, the commission sees in the bioeconomy a convergence of opportunities and objectives: a smart use of our biological resources from land and seas; a low-carbon, resource-efficient economy; a reindustrialisation of europe based on innovation and the latest scientific knowledge; food security for all; and the development of new jobs and new sources of economic growth, not least in rural and maritime regions. all these aspects are especially relevant in the context of the economic difficulties currently facing europe. since the adoption of the bioeconomy strategy and action plan in early 2012, considerable progress has been made. the bioeconomy is still developing, so one of our important objectives has been to establish a bioeconomy observatory, to provide policy-makers, primary producers, industry and other stakeholders with authoritative, up-to-date information about relevant research, policy, and market developments. this is the first time in the world that an observatory of this kind has been set up. it will require the positive engagement of many different organisations to make this initiative a success. the commission’s joint research centre is already working hard to get the observatory up and running and producing results. we have also committed to establish a bioeconomy panel, to facilitate discussion, joint actions and exchange of experience between different stakeholder groups: researchers, producers, industry, civil society, and public administrations at regional, national and eu level. the 30 members of the panel have been selected, and the first meeting is scheduled to take place in september. i am pleased to confirm our invitation to parliament to nominate an observer to this bioeconomy panel. this will help to further consolidate the alignment between our two institutions on issues related to the bioeconomy. in february this year we organised, together with the irish presidency, the second annual european stakeholders’ conference on the bioeconomy, bringing together over 500 people representing a wide variety of different interests related to the bioeconomy. we are grateful to meps paolo bartolozzi and mairead mcguinness for the valuable contributions that they made to this event. many of the conclusions of the conference are echoed in the report that you are debating today, such as the need for a coherent, coordinated policy; the need for investments in skills and training; and, the need for transparent and inclusive dialogue to ensure that the bioeconomy is built on broad-based public support. we look forward to working with the italian presidency of the eu in organising the next conference in the second half of 2014. as you all know, just last week the european parliament and council, together with the commission, reached political agreement on horizon 2020 – the next funding programme for research, innovation and science. let me assure you that within horizon 2020 there will be a substantial budget for bioeconomy-related research and innovation. this will include a significant proportion of funding for a new public- private partnership (ppp) on bio-based industries. the commission very much appreciates the clear support that the parliament report gives to this ppp and to the bioeconomy research budget as a whole. this ppp in particular will help to finance pilot and demonstration activities of the kind that the draft resolution calls for. finally, i would like to underline that the commission is very pleased that the draft resolution repeats the call to eu member states to develop their own national and regional bioeconomy strategies. i could not agree more. while there is much we can and will do at an eu level, the bioeconomy will only realise its full potential if actors at national and regional level understand the opportunities that this presents for them and put in place the appropriate policies, funding, and governance mechanisms.

president of the european council. − mr president, honourable members, after the march european council meeting i reported to you on the broad agreement among all leaders on our strategy to bring the european union to recovery: first, restoring and maintaining financial stability; second, making our economies more resilient and competitive, with structurally sound public finances (using the flexibilities in our common rules) and long-term reforms; third, fighting, directly and indirectly, unemployment, and i added explicitly, especially for the young; and the fourth element of our strategy was working towards a genuine economic and monetary union – preparing for the future. looking back at the decisions taken at or just before the june european council – because sometimes the pressure created by having a european council meeting can concentrate minds – it is striking to see that on each and every one of the four strands of this strategy we are moving forward, we are making progress – gradually, but decisively. as is now the tradition every june, we discussed and endorsed the country-specific recommendations, thus closing this year’s european semester, which is the cornerstone of our new economic governance. though only three years old, it is already the most advanced surveillance and policy coordination mechanism in the world. we welcomed the agreement reached by finance ministers the night before the european council on the directive on recovery and resolution. this is a crucial matter, which can now be taken forward with parliament in the legislative process before the end of this parliamentary term. together with the single supervisory mechanism and the directive on capital requirements (where parliament’s efforts to finalise the legislative work have been of vital importance), this directive on resolution and recovery is essential for the completion of the banking union, which is a key element of the work on a genuine economic and monetary union. the banking union remains an immediate priority – and the european council stressed this again forcefully – as it will help ensure financial stability, reduce financial fragmentation and restore normal lending to the economy. on the latter point – restoring normal lending to the economy – european leaders also took action and we agreed on an investment plan for europe, based on a joint report by the commission and the european investment bank. the aim is to address the credit crunch that is holding back the very companies that should be driving the recovery: local smes, and the start-ups of today which will perhaps be the success stories of tomorrow. we need to bring oxygen deep into the system, across the whole union, and especially in the most vulnerable countries. we also agreed on concrete measures with an immediate impact to fight youth unemployment, which is a most urgent concern for our societies – and a concern we also discussed in the presence of the european social partners in a prime example of social dialogue at work at eu level. we decided to scale up and speed up the youth employment initiative, so that the money starts flowing as of 1 january 2014. most of the money will now be spent in 2014-2015, the years when it is most needed; moreover, the flexibility offered by the mff means, in effect, that there will be substantially more available for the youth employment initiative than the eur 6 billion we had initially foreseen for it; according to projections at least eur 8 billion in total. we made a clear link between this youth employment initiative and the youth guarantee – to ensure that within four months of leaving school or becoming unemployed, every young person gets a good offer for a job, education or training. we also called for other important actions – for instance promoting cross-border mobility through the eures and erasmus+ programmes, including vocational training, as well as high-quality apprenticeships. these measures will undoubtedly boost the efforts taken by national governments, with which the bulk of the responsibility lies. during the european council it was clear that leaders are eager to exchange experiences and best practices, just as they will again at tomorrow’s meeting in berlin. the decisions that the european council took just a couple of days ago on the financing of the economy and the fight against youth unemployment would not have been possible without the agreement reached on the multiannual financial framework by the presidents of the parliament, the council and the commission just a couple of hours before the start of the european council. last thursday, the european council unanimously and firmly gave its political backing to the mff agreement. based on that, member state representatives have, in the meantime, formally approved it. i hope that you will equally approve the mff later this week. it will be a catalyst for investment and growth and jobs across europe – which is particularly urgent and necessary at a time of crisis, a time of high unemployment and of doubts about the european project. indeed, the best way to restore confidence and prove these doubts wrong is by showing that europe is delivering, that we are leaving a difficult situation behind and can jointly cope with the challenges of the future. of course, there is still a lot of work ahead of us, on many fronts – for instance on the deepening of economic and monetary union, on which i gave heads of government a detailed state of play last friday. but this should not prevent us from reaffirming loud and clear that, even if the road is still long, we are on the right track and that when our institutions work together for the common european good – and the mff is an example – europe is capable of producing concrete, tangible results. as i have just said, we are producing results, and last week proved it. the june european council also proved that our european project remains attractive for those who are not yet part of it. on friday morning, we agreed to move forward towards opening accession talks with serbia, and to take an important step in our relations with kosovo. we welcomed croatia as a member of the european union and latvia as a member of the eurozone. so, we are welcoming new members, and not – as some had predicted – over recent months and years, the european union has made an impressive and unprecedented effort to stabilise the euro and adapt our structures and policies to meet the challenges posed by the crisis. we still have a lot of work to do, however, before we can leave the crisis behind. as i said to the european council last week: the crisis is not over. we should not let up in our efforts for stability and growth by completing the emu, correcting our public finances, structural reforms for competitiveness and targeted investments for growth. the june european council was precisely about everyone taking up their responsibilities. it has delivered some very important results: by endorsing the country-specific recommendations for structural reforms as proposed by the commission, by stepping up the fight against youth unemployment, and by taking decisions aimed at restoring normal lending to the real economy, notably to smes. i have to mention first one result that was achieved a by you and by the council. the extremely challenging dynamics of the negotiation process – unanimity in the council, consent by absolute majority at parliament – mean that nobody was able to reach all of their objectives. this is why – even though the commission has always supported a more ambitious european budget – i consider this agreement a crucial step for the european union in demonstrating its capacity to act and to take difficult decisions. the eu budget is an almost one trillion euro investment fund for growth and jobs. without it, everything we are trying to do for growth, for investment, for the regions, for young people, for employment and for research would be put at risk. in terms of the structural reforms needed to get our socio-economic framework in line with the demands of today’s global economy, the agenda was set out clearly in the annual growth survey and, in particular, in the country-specific recommendations presented by the commission five weeks ago. with the endorsement of these recommendations by the european council, a new step was taken in the european semester process. economic governance in the european union has reached a new stage of maturity and common ownership. everyone can now see that this is not a top-down process with the commission telling members what to do. but governments now should accept that reform, or lack of reform, in one country seriously impacts on neighbours and economic partners across europe, and sometimes across the world. we are all in this together, so we have to cooperate, coordinate, debate and decide together as well. this is what economic union means. this is economic governance at work. and it is working. now, we have to make our common efforts to work to tackle some of the social and economic challenges we are facing together – youth unemployment especially. most of the groundwork to turn this economically untenable and socially unacceptable situation around must be done at national level. therefore, the commission has proposed specific recommendations on youth unemployment for 19 countries: from reforming labour markets to reinforcing public employment services, from shifting taxation away from labour to improving education for the low-skilled, or supporting programmes for training and apprenticeships. there is a lot that national governments can and must do. i welcome the fact that the european council has clearly underlined that message. now governments must honour their commitments. the european institutions are there to guide and support this effort, in particular through the structural funds: we will speed up the youth employment initiative and front-load the funds so that the initial eur 6 billion is invested in the following two years, and not spread thinly over the full seven years of the mff period. if we want this money to really make a difference, we need to focus it on regions with youth unemployment rates of over 25%, and do so quickly. this is only possible if member states prepare specific youth unemployment initiative programmes and submit their plans this year. this will enable us to hit the ground running early in 2014. and as this house rightly stressed in the mff discussions, we need to guarantee funds for the years afterwards as well. so now – thanks to the increased flexibility that the european commission has always supported and that was finally agreed by the member states – the total amount spent on youth unemployment over the seven years can be estimated at above eur 8 billion. we also need to re-launch and expand the youth employment action teams. since we set them up early in 2012, these teams have helped eight member states reallocate around eur 16 billion in structural funds to the most pressing needs, to the benefit of about one million young people and 55 000 smes. the new teams will be sent to help countries prepare their youth employment initiative projects and implement the youth guarantee scheme. on top of this, we will boost the mobility of young workers – one of the unfulfilled promises of the internal market so far – by reforming eures, which already gives access to over 1.4 million vacancies in europe and nearly 31 000 registered employers across the european union. later today, in the margins of the worldskills competition in leipzig, the european commission will launch another important initiative, following the grand coalition for digital jobs we set up earlier. we will launch today the european alliance for apprenticeships, because not everything can be done by governments or other public institutions. we should also mobilise the social partners. business can do more to help create more and better quality apprenticeships. before the european council together with some twenty heads of state and government and labour ministers, we are also meeting with the president of the european parliament, in berlin, to add to the momentum of the fight against youth unemployment. all taken together, i would say: finally youth employment as a top priority seems an idea whose time has come. but ideas are not enough. our young people need actions, they need decisions, and they need jobs. so let us do it. the june european council also made measures to support financing to small and medium-sized enterprises a priority. i welcome that, on the basis of the recommendations in the joint report by the commission and the eib, the european council has supported much-needed action in this field. following the increase of its capital – that we were the first to advocate – the extra eib activities are expected to increase its lending activity in the eu by at least 40% between 2013 and 2015, with a particular focus on innovation and skills, sme financing, resource efficiency and strategic infrastructure. in our joint report with the eib, the european commission has outlined a number of options for launching ambitious joint risk-sharing financial instruments to leverage private-sector and capital-market investments in smes in the very near future. our proposals aim at fully exploiting the joint potential of the structural funds, together with loans from the eib. the european council committed member states to do their part of the further preparatory work in order for these instruments to be fully operational by january 2014. it was also year. with our communication on the ‘top ten’ consultation of smes, we urge all parties involved to take a long hard look at themselves to see if their role in legislation is a burden or a help to smes. we should always try to lighten the load of regulation, where possible, without lowering our standards or losing sight of the agreed common european goals. i believe these are the key issues that determine, in the short term, both the effectiveness and the legitimacy of our reform efforts. with the compact for jobs and growth we wanted to pool and reinforce the broader agenda of measures follow-up to the compact for growth has been a mixed success. there have been some real breakthroughs, such as the recent agreement on professional qualifications and public procurement, but in other areas progress has been uneven or simply too slow. we must speed up work on the single market act proposals, on the digital single market, the internal energy market and the european research area. time is running out, so i hope to be able to count on your persistent and powerful support to push through as much of our growth and jobs agenda as possible by the end of the term of this parliament. point i would like to make concerns the deepening of the economic and monetary union. one of the main reasons why we have been able to overcome the existential threat to the euro is that the european institutions and member states have signalled their determination to learn the lessons of the crisis, to complete the emu, and to make it irreversible. we cannot backtrack on that promise. the only way is forward, as set out in our blueprint towards a deep and genuine emu. but sometimes we receive conflicting signals on the political will to move further. last week we saw an important breakthrough with the council’s agreement on a common approach to dealing with failing banks without relying on taxpayers’ money. the commission is now looking forward to working closely with and i hope that we can make swift progress on that. this will ensure effective european decision-making on problematic banks within the single supervisory mechanism. the forthcoming implementation of the two-pack takes us one step closer to a fiscal union. today i would like to announce that, following our commitment towards the european parliament as part of the overall agreement on the two-pack, the commission is now setting up an expert group to look into all merits and risks, the legal requirements and the financial consequences of initiatives of joint issuance of debt in the form of a in writing. only strong and far-reaching measures that restore confidence and put europe on the path to strong, smart, sustainable and inclusive growth will enable us to overcome the current economic and financial crisis. among the various measures agreed, i would like to highlight the decisions taken to combat youth unemployment, which has reached dramatic proportions, with some 5 million young people unemployed in europe, and as a result of which we are in grave danger of seeing a whole generation grow up without any real prospects for the future. i welcome the financial reinforcement provided for under the youth employment initiative. i am afraid that the budgetary shortfalls resulting from the council's myopia and british imposition are not up to the challenges we have to face. member states should make efforts to adapt the training of young people to the real needs of the labour market, for example by introducing new traineeships and training which will enable young people to enter the labour market better prepared. at the same time, they should encourage greater dynamism and competitiveness in the labour market, for example by introducing tax incentives for the recruitment of young people. measures to support entrepreneurship and to strengthen the erasmus+ and erasmus first employment european programmes were also approved.
in writing. on 27 and 28 june, the heads of state or government of the 27 european countries agreed on a number of measures to promote youth employment, latvia's accession to the euro area and economic and monetary union. i would like to emphasize the results achieved in the area of youth employment, due to the fact that the european institutions have finally adopted a resolution with concrete measures that can be applied in most member states. at a time when the average rate of youth unemployment in europe is already over 23% and in some countries over 60%, i believe it is urgent to implement new measures to promote youth employment, such as promoting increased mobility at european level, reducing the gap between higher education and the needs of the labour market, or supporting venture capital firms, business angels or the creation of business incubators that stimulate young entrepreneurship. finally, i would also call on the member states to reduce corporate taxes for companies when they hire a significant number of young people, reducing the unemployment rate and the social costs associated with it and increasing the capacity for innovation and technological leadership.

the irish presidency comes to an end with the conclusion of the agreement between the presidents of the three institutions parliament, council and commission on the proposal for the multiannual financial framework 2014-2020. as expected and as we have warned, after the appropriate theatricalisation, with vows that they would never approve the council's proposal for a multiannual financial framework, the right wing and the social democrats in parliament have agreed to conclude an agreement which represents a complete concession to the great powers who are leading the integration process. after agreeing to the adoption of the budget treaty, which perpetuates the so-called austerity policies, the social democrats came to say that the strengthening of discipline would be matched by a strengthening of solidarity, expressed in a strengthening of the eu budget. this is what the socialist party in portugal did and said, joining the right as usual. the significance of the european solidarity so widely espoused is once again clear. for the first time, the community budget is being reduced in absolute terms, even in the context of a new enlargement. at a time when inequalities and divergences between countries are increasing, cohesion funds are being cut. portugal will lose about 10% of eu funding compared to the current financial framework. and it will lose even more with the deepening of this capitalist integration.
in writing. - i welcome this report, taking into account that the current economic environment offers a good opportunity to modernise the staff regulations of officials of the european union so that they better reflect the demographic and economic reality of europe. however, i think it is essential that the principles underlying a sound and modern personnel policy in the european institutions be based in particular on the need to reward performance and quality of service and to take account of geographical balance. the rapporteur believes, and i agree, that these principles should be at the heart of the new reform and that any changes should also ensure the fairness of the european union system, reflect the efforts to consolidate national administrations and the conditions offered by other international organisations.
in writing. the report under review, by mrs dagmar roth-behrendt, deals with the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending the staff regulations of officials and the conditions of employment of other servants of the european union. the economic and financial crisis requires fiscal consolidation in the member states. so this moment should be an opportunity not only for them to reduce their spending on the public sector but also to make the public administration much more efficient. the european institutions must be a reference in terms of human resource management, by hiring independent and highly qualified staff. i therefore welcome this initiative to reduce the budget lines for staff and to redirect financial resources towards productive investments that promote economic growth and job creation. because this is a resolution which aims to provide the european institutions with a sound and modern personnel policy which, in addition to taking account of geographical balance, is based on the criteria of competence and quality, i voted in favour.
in writing. − the eu institutions and agencies together employ some 55 000 officials and other staff. the philosophy of this report is clearly to legitimize the view/myth that the economic crisis is directly or indirectly due to an excess of workers' rights and, as such, also to legitimize the subsidiary political practice of this view, which is to attack workers in their rights and wages. this fact alone conditions and determines our position against the report. this reform - which has been opposed by workers, who have undertaken various measures of struggle, including strikes - will, they say, save a total of 8 billion euros at the expense of workers' wages and pensions. the commission proposes to reduce the staff of each institution and agency by 5%. the rapporteur acknowledges (and accepts) that, while the objectives and the workload are maintained, this cut implies that each worker will take on a share of the additional workload. other proposed savings measures include the increase in working hours without compensation in terms of pay, the increase in the retirement age from 63 to 65 years, the elimination of the expatriation allowance. we voted against it.

in writing. − the institutions and agencies located in the different eu places of work and their delegations in third countries employ, in total, some 55 000 officials and other staff. the reform of the staff regulations and the european civil service introduced in 2004 has made it possible to modernise them and improve their cost-effectiveness. this reform will result in savings totalling eur 8 billion by the end of 2020. the main objective of this proposal is to introduce a new method of adjusting wages and pensions, including the application of the exception clause and the special contribution. in this time of crisis, we must all contribute to combating it, hence my vote in favour.

in writing. − taking into account, on the one hand, the expiry at the end of 2012 of the applicable provisions of the staff regulations and, on the other, the need to respond to the judgment of the court of justice in case c-40/10, the commission has timely submitted the proposal aimed at introducing a new method of adjusting salaries and pensions, including the application of the exception clause and the special contribution. the proposal is being presented in the context of the financial crisis in europe and incorporates the savings measures contained in all the budget lines in the multiannual financial framework. the rapporteur therefore concludes that the amendments contribute to the balance between the realisation of savings and the need to ensure that the institutions carry out the tasks entrusted to them in accordance with the obligations and powers laid down in the treaties. in view of the rapporteur's assessment, i voted in favour of the report on the staff regulations of officials of the european union.

in writing. - i approve this report, taking into account that international civil liability in nuclear matters is governed by two instruments: the vienna convention and the 1960 paris convention on the civil liability of third parties in the field of nuclear energy. both conventions share similar principles as regards substance. the vienna convention was adopted to provide adequate and fair compensation to victims of damage caused by nuclear accidents by creating a special civil liability system in the field of nuclear energy. the union therefore has exclusive competence with regard to those provisions contained in the protocol and member states cannot become contracting parties to the protocol with regard to those provisions. in order to address the remaining lack of uniformity between member states as regards the rules governing the procedure for the recognition and enforcement of judgments in the field of nuclear damage, i welcome the commission's decision to commit to considering the extension, in a future proposal, of the solution of giving precedence to union rules to the member states which ratified the 1997 protocol prior to their accession to the european union, namely latvia and romania, and to the member states which are contracting parties to the paris convention.
